OWD JEMMY. What! never knowed owd Jemmy, lad, PP As use' to live up yon— Kept hens, and wooav o' th' owd hand looms ? . Well, tha'art a bonny mon ! AW'll bet there wornd a single sowl Fro here to th' end o' t' looan, As dudnd wish owd Jemmy wed. Or mourn when he wer gooan! Aw've set on t' seatbooard many a heawr, Wol he booath wooav an' sung, Or ceawrd bi' th' fire, an' herkend t' tales As he spun off his tongue. He'd toke o' th' cruel Corn Law days, :4 When fieawr wer sixpence t' peawnd, 77- An' t' corn wer kept fro' t' starvin' poor, Then chucked i' t' sea unseawnd. Iv tha'rt a Tory, dornd be mad At wod aw'm beawn to tell : He often said as Tory laws Were med bi "him i' hell"! Thad's rayther strong; but th' Corn Law days Hed robbed him ov his mam, An' left him, an' some moor beside, To work an' cry' at? clam. Sometimes he'd hey a noisy lot 0' mmpin' laughing lads Set reawnd his fire, wol he towd tales Abeawt their youthful dads— Wed fun they hed, wod tricks they played, When he wer in his prime— Aw'm sure he welly med th' lads ill WP laffin, mony a time. Bud mooast ov o' owd Jemmy luvd A pratty little child, P - Id mattered nowt wod troubled him, Iv he si one he smiled; He'd welly awlus one hi' th' hand When ramblin' to an' fro, • An' t' youngsters seemed to think as he Wer t' grandad to urn o'. Toart th' latter end he used to say He'd bi content to dee, Iv he 'nut sit at "Heaven's doer" WP a child on oather knee. An' when his life wer goin deawn, Like th' ocean's ebbin' tide, He couldn'd be contented till They browt one to his side. 7-• He passed away Pt' summer time, r When fleawrs wer o' 1' bloom, An' th' owd sun brooak through t' cleawds d' giet • As hung o'er o' th' room_ Tha thinks his sowl's at rest? " Ay sure, ! An' bee bin many a day. For sich a good owd heart as his Could ne'er go far astray." GEORGE HULL. Higher Walton, July 26th, lEST.

A tender-hearted and compassionate disposition which inclines men to pity and feel the misfortunes of others, and which is even for its awn sake incapable of involv- ng any man in ruin and misery, is of all tempers of mind the most amiable, and, though it never receives much honoutis worthy of the highest. To be too independent with those we love is a mistake te be carefully avoided, for excessive independence is a 'barrier that checkslyrnpathy as effectually as a rugged shoulder stopsthe even flow of a limpid stream. To yield a little, taking and giving trifling services, not only , affords mutual pleasure, but serves to dra.vt closer the 'silken threads of love, the tension of which,. even with bur most intimate ones, is apt somewhat to slacken, needing careful watching lest the threads snap entirely. Whittling is a special malady of the American brain, developed particularly in the West, where there are few men who do not manifest these symptoms. Its diagnosis consists in an irresistible desire to take in the left hand is piece of wood and to reduce it to morsels of the size of a match by a gentle and regular movement of the right hand armed with a pocket knife, a razor, or a bowie-knife. The indulgence of this pro- pensity sometimes facilitates, but more frequently re- places, conversation, according to temperament; but the predisposition—quite as imperious as the passion for opium among the Chinese—is no more easily explained than a taste for olives, or dominoes, or rancid bacon, or why Schiller could not get on with his work without the smell of rotten apples under his nose. It seems that at Washington formerly they used to deliver to each senator or deputy, at the commencement of their sitting, a little block of cedar and a penknife, furnished by the questor- ship for this purpose; they had found this to be the most effective remedy for preserving the arms of the chairs, which, formerly, never lasted out a session- The epidemic being oaths decline in the Eastern States at present, I hear that paper-knives, provided they are replaced frequently, answer all the purpose of securing the preservation of the public furniture. As a conscientious observer, I wished to account for the sensations, evidently volup- tuous, which my neighbours, absorbed in this occupation, appeared to feel. Accordingly, I asked one of them to give me a practical lesson, that I might study the phenomenon. Be was a cow-boy, getting gray, orna- mented with a Babylonian beard, and armed with two formidable revolvers. Tearing from the bench a piece, six inches long, he offered his services most courteously. This fragment I took, and leaning one end of it against the pit of my stomach, I began, with his own bowie- knife which he lent me, cutting it into thin splinters, much more equal and regular than the matches turned out by the French regie. Encouraged by the kind glances which this homage rendered to the customs of the country won for me from the company, I continued to the end, and I am sorry to say I found no gratification whatever in the experiment; on the contrary, a disagree- able sensation in the lower region of the stomach, which reminded me of the horrible mal de mer I once had with the first cigar I smoked with the Reverends Peres Jesuites. Perhaps I ought to have remembered that the stomach is a highly sensitive organ, and ill-adapted to resist external pressure when there is nothing within, and should have taken a "drop" to ensure success.—Cotv- Boys and Colanel.4. THE QUEEN AND THE COTTAGER.

The following beautiful anecdote of Her Majesty is taken from an old paper. The incident referred to is said to have occurred at Osborne soon after the Queen became a widow:— Her Majesty was fond, in those days, of welkin..' in quiet places, without friend or attendant. One day having passed the gate of her park, she discovered a pleasant-looking lane which she had never visited. She turned into the new path and walked on until, coming to a little thatched cottage, she heard a loud voice speak- ing in unusual tones. The sounds were so uncertain the listener could not tell whether they meant distress or disagreement. Moved by a desire to know, she paused, and then knocked at the door. The voice within re- sponded—" C,eme in." The Queen lifted the latchstring and entered a room where an aged woman lay upon a bed. No other person was in the house. The visitor remarked, as if in apology for her intrusion, that she thought someone might be in distress, and kindly inquired if anything was the matter. The woman replied that nothing was the matter, and invited the stranger to sit down. Then, as the visitor's questions drew her on, she told her little story. She had been bedridden, so she said, for eight years, and she was dependent upon her daughter's earnings for the most of her living. The daughter was errand-woman , to a rich family not far away, and as she was gone from . morning until night, the mother must stay alone all day, , unless some good neighbour came in to say a kind word. , She could not read at all, but every morning her daughter , read a chapter from the Bible, and she repeated to herself, ; when alone, such verses as she could remember, for corn- . patsy. Her repeating from this morning's chapter was , what the stranger heard from outside. The book of Psalms lay on the bed, and the old invalid asked her visitor if she wouldn't find the place her daughter had , last read, as she couldn't remember her verse quite rightly to-day. The place was found and the Psalm read from the beginning, until the invalid exclaimed—" That's the verse, that's it !" and her mind was satisfied with its por- tion of the word of God. Just as the reading was finished there was a knock at , the door, and directly two young women bounced into the room. The lady sitting there was very plainly dressed in simple black, with an old-looking straw bonnet upon her head. The young women, with too much haste for courtesy, brushed past the stranger and stood by the bed. They talked -eagerly, as people do who are in a great hustle over some unexpected event. They inquired how the old cottager did, and wished to know if she were pro- vided for in certain ways, and if she had eaten all the nice things they had previously brought. They couldn't stay to-day, for there was to be a fête in honour of the Queen to-morrow, and they were busy in preparing to attend. They counted greatly upon seeing their Queen. Telling the old woman she must let them know it she wanted anything, they brushed past the silent stranger again, and rushed out of the door. When they were quite gone, the unknown lady asked the invalid who her young visitors might be, and she learned that they were the daughters of a man of some note in the neighbourhood whom she knew very well. After a little more pleasant talk the straneer rose to go. As she was leaving she put a sovereign in the invalid's hand, and said she would some time visit her again. The money was accepted with deep thankfulness and stream- ing eyes. " My young ladies, when they come again, will want to know who you are," she said; "what shall I tell them?" With a pleasant smile the visitor answered—] "I am the Queen of England I" The helpless creature almost rose from her bed at the words. That visit was a wonderful memory ever after- wards. She told every one who called at her cottage the beautiful story of her Sovereign reading the Bible to her, always emphasising the wonder that she, in her poor cottage, should ever see the Queen. •

Hyacinth, who noticed everYthing and forgot nothing, knew' that in the barn were some stacks of corn, and she had formed the bold resolve of concealing herself behind these. THE WARRINGTON GAS WORKS. Sir,—l see Mr. F. Dixon calls the attention of the publin to a matter which is little less than a grave scandal, viz.: the utter impossibility to raise a discussion in the Council chamber on the management of the Gas Works. Surely the Gas Committee know what is due to themselves as public servants, and can have no private ends to serve by burking full and open criticism of their doings. Times without number Councillor Dixon has essayed to bring charges of one kind or another before the chamber, hut only to be met by some master of jibes and sneers. It is time this was stopped, and full opportunity offered for reviewing the work of the Gas Committee since the time of the purchase of the works. Whatever gain may accrue to posterity, at least the present generation is receiving no profit, either in the way of cheap gas, or in the way of good ILLUMINATION THE NEW LES —,RINGTON

use is eminently conducive to excellence and vigour." I submit, sir, that testimony of this kind pub- lished in a paper of (ILA weight and standing, far outweighs the evidence geuerally offered to us—the masses. It has been urged that "the chief effect of teetotal so- cieties is purely mischievous, by causing weak people, who would be better for a little alcohol, to abstain from it to their injury." The truth is that the general opinion of medical men is expressed by the fact that only a very few of them are total abstainers.

What I urge upon the teetotaller, is the full recognition a the weakness of human nature, that the sur- roundings of men and women shall be considered ; in abort that cause and effect frilly at work shall be taken into account in the efforts put forth to reclaim the drunkard. In nearly all cases it is the diminished self-control of insipient insanity which leads to drink, and not drink which leads to insanity. I was much struck by an essay in the " Contem- porary" of April, 1877. in which the writer says—" It is a 'fair question whether we may not be bound to keep tempta- 'lion to drink out of the way of those whom it maddens, just as we keep razors from children." When people get drunk persistently and miserably, so as to come under the classification of confirmed inebriates, and I must acknow- ledge to a narrow acquaintance of this sort, it is difficult to give a reason for it, but one reason may be. to use the words of Mr. Walter Besant, that there are "thousands of men and women continually occupied in miserable toil for wretched wages, who never venture to hope for any cessation or re- laxation of the life sentence to which they were doomed at I their birth."

It is often asserted that drunkenness and crime go hand in hand. That this is not so, Pro. Leone Levi has shown conclusively by his comparisons drawn from the several beer drinking countries. We can never tolerate grandmotherly legislation; the days for sumptuary laws are past, and all alike must look for the cause of drunkenness and its cure in the utterly senseless way in which society in its various parts lacks co- hesion. Education, sanitary improvements, better dwellings for the poorer classes, and strange as it may seem, less in- terference with the publicans, are the remedies. Instead of making the publican a pariab, we must claim his help, prove to him that adulteration and drunkenness will not benefit him, and then we shall be on the right track. CLIFFORD DIX.

THE FREE LIBRARY QUESTION. Sir,—The thanks of my fellow townsmen are due to you for your untiring advocacy at this question. I was pleased to see your late article and the letters of your correspon- dents. The matter must not be allowed to drop. Having put our hands to the plough we will not look back but will continue the fight till success crowns our efforts. Un- doubtedly the two committees must unite, and I would sug- gest an early meeting with that object. We must convince the "powers that be" that we are thoroeghly in earnest and that we are backed up with the town at large. It is nothing less than a scandal that things have been allowed to go on so long in the manner they have. Public houses are at every street corner, and facilities are provided with the utmost profuseness for men to spend their leisure hours in a manner that entails great waste of their means, and consequent curtailment of comfort, and even neces- saries for their families. But if a man wants to spend his leisure bourn in a manner that will be profitable to himself and conduce to the respect of others—he must needs trudga from whatever part of the town he may reside—after a hard day's work—to Bold-street—and then just as he has got comfortably settled to a book, to be turned out at nine o'clock. Same years ago, when parliament passed an early closing bill and public-houses were compelled to close at eleven o'clock, we beard a good deal about grandmotherly government. But what grandmotherly notions our local rulers have? Well, dr, discarding the sneers about "band of enthu- siasts." and "intellectual zealots," we must act as " CH& ford Dix" suggests. and make this a test question for the let of November. We have a number of councillors on our side, and I don't despair of our winning over the rest—but failing that, we will run candidates of our own. I hope, however, we shall be spared such a neceesity.—Yours, JOHN GANDY.

THE TEMPERANCE MOVEMENT. Sir,—Like those of his kidney who stick a bit of blue ribbon in their coats, "J. J. Langham " burns to advertise his virtues, or he would not have published the "milk and water vanity" appearing above his name in your last issue. Tls based in charity—that men are brothers. And those who make a fuss, About their temperance thus. Are not so much more temperate than others." I would also remark that Mr. Longhorn, when in London. made shocking bad use of his time, orbs would have known the difference between what he calls "epithets" and what be imagines to be "Billingsgate." But his ignorance re- specting the brewing trade there is even more crass ; so crass that he does not venture to touch upon my reply on the public-house question in the metropolis. And why ? Because be knows nothing about it; although in "sheer impertinence" (no Billingsgate here!) he published an opinion on it. His dictum that the poor drink a quart of beer to the rich man's pint. is another of these absurd notions that have got possession of his soul ; and on ideas like these he will rush into print! And he tells me in language worthy of Solomon, to "Learn then, my 'Uncle Toby,' &c., ecc and a little more drivel of that sort. It is pitiful stuff to have to reply to; but thank the gods, he says he will not write any more on the subject. This is as it should be. I may just notice one more phrase of Mr. Longhorn's before closing. He says—" He might well decline to reason with such a man as Uncle Toby.'" It would have been well if he bad ; for although he floundered about rich brewers and poverty in his first letter' he absolutely lost himself in his last. And although both his epistles are full of ignorant assertions (as I know them to be) yet, with that cool ardour so characteristic of the bigots on his side, he goes on condemning others who differ from him ; and is landed in exactly the same position as a critic who runs down an author, a single line of whose works he has never read. And se I leave him. 'Why should I give him two black eyes for being blind? "—Yours faithfully, UNCLE TOBY.

At last eawr Tura fotched un owd blunderbus fro' deawnstairs us wur his grond- fayther's, un foyert into th' back yerd, but it wus aw at no yoos. Th' hallelooya korus wus con- tinued. He skryked same us a. jay, un wot wi owd ' Bangum's din un th' cats fyren away harder then ' ever, aw thowt eawr Turn wud ha gon off his churitp.. Whey, eawr Turn sed, theau greight bledder-yed, , connot theau beer thoos hinfernal cats maykin thare din? Aw've hovven very near everythin ith' heawse at hum,-but aw connot stop urn. Theer they gooa, theer they gooa, sheawted eawr Turn, an wons agen he waltzed reawnd reawm in a positiv frenzy. Ger eawt, the,aw greight foo, sed Billy Bangum, thoos is not cats at aw. CONSECRATION or A BisHop.---On Wednesday, being St. Bartholomew's Day, the same festival on which, ten years ago, his predecessor was consecrated in the same place, the Archbishop of York consecrated in York Minster 1 the Venerable James Waring Bardsley, Archdeacon of Liverpool, to the Bishopric of Sodor and Man. There was a large attendance of clergy, especially from the Liverpool diocese, where the Archdeacon has long laboured. The preacher was the Rev. Herbert James.

div.head: TEMPERANCE QUESTION.
div.p: THE TEMPERANCE QUESTION.

Sir,—The very great importance of the temperance ques- tion must be toy excuse for troubling your readers further respecting it. Allow me first to acknowledge my satisfac- tion with Mr. Longhorn's temperate and civil manner of dealing with his critics. If I cannot say the same of Mr. W. Roberts it is because Ido not wish to give him credit for what he does not deserve. I think temperance, so far as actually drinking beer is concerned, is about the only bit he has in his whole constitution and if he should lose that, things might go awkward with him. I take it, sir, that the question of making people sober is second in importance to none, and when an opportunity is offered in the columns of a newspaper for its healthy venti-, lotion it is mere cowardice to shirk it by saying that "op- portunities are so few, and time is so precious." Mr. W. Roberts "doubts my sympathy with the movement." There is nothing strange in this; it is one of his character- istics to doubt other people; hence his tactical blunders.

Now, sir, my first statement was a general one, to the effect that the Temperance Federation was made up of people who were not total abstainers, and I am of opinion that remarks made on a platform of such a character should be temperate and conciliating. Mr. Roberts and Mr. Yonge may think different.

The teetotallers have, perhaps, been led into their present intemperate state through a sort of indifference on the part of the public to criticise their wild statements when reported in the newspaper. All the same, moderate men turn away from these statements with a sneer, and refuse to give such help as might otherwise be expected in the attempts made to reclaim the weak and ill-developed creatures who have fallen into the vg,ye of drunkenness. . . _

Curiously enouih, I And in your columns full confirma- tion ef my assertion that abstainers are not making head- way in their efforts to persuade the people to do that which is altogether against nature, that is, to at once and suddenly forswear the use of alcohol. Mrs. Parker, tbe "foremost woman in the temperance CIUSO in the world," says:—"l find that the temperance movement is winning new ad- herents, but I also find that the liquor traffic is advancing Immeasurably faster." Speaking of America, she is forced to confess "that the liquor business has fairly made leaps and bounds." In Great Britain and America it is pretty much the same—" liquor has far outdistanced temperance of late years." lam Sorry to have to reproduce these words, but no good will Le done by smothering the fact that there *in man from the highest to the lowest a desire for a stimulant. This desire and the palate together find their satisfaction in the drinking of alcoholic liquors. If drunken. ness, like gluttony, was limited in its action, and could bs a hidden instead of an open vice, we should hear little of it, but it is— _

The thoughts that snring Out of human suffering' that causes the voice to speak. Sir W. Roberts tells us that malt liquors, provided they are sound and free from acidity, interfere but little with salivary digestion ; and that a moderate quantity of light beer, when "well up," is favourable to stomach digestion. His strongest condemnations are reserved for the alternative drinks offered to US by our abstaining friends, tea, coffee, &c. Dr. Sutton Sharpe, speaking of Sir Henry Thompson, says "when I have had the pleasure and benefit or consulting him, al- though be has advised moderation in all things, total ab- stinence has formed no Part."

Evidence in abundance exists, and may be culled from medical journals, articles, and speeches, and all of a ten- dency inculcating moderation in the use of alcohol. In an article in the' Times" of August 14th, 1884, the propo- sition was laid down "that alcohol, as an element of diet, and when used in moderate quantity, is a highly economical force generator, a fuel that is fit to burn for the support of the system without any previous preparation by the diges- tive organs, and that for the majority of mankind, and es-

div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.

HOUSE OF COMMONSattraner. . 1 The Speaker took the chair at 12.20 p.m. , SUPPLY: EGYPTIAN POLICY. - - The House went into Committee of Supply.—On the 'Diplomatic Vote of £234,524, Sir G. CAMPBELL moved , "the reduction of the vote by £5OO in order to raise the "question of our occupatlon of Egypt, against the con- tinuance of which he protested as being unnecessary for the protection of British interests in the East and in- eurious to the Egyptians. . Mr. BRYCE blamed the Government for beginning these hegotiaeions for a settlement of the question at Paris in- if- stead of at Constantinople, and for countenancing a ioint occupation of Egypt with the Turks. He denied reel any benefit had been derived from the recent nego- tiations, and, challenging the Government to say when ,they intended to leave the country, taunted them with mconsistency in their former declarations. Sir J. Feeorrssoe repudiated the suggestion that the Government had been inconsistent. They were doing reen in their power to alleviate the burdens of the c•ffeptian people and to maintain order, but it was im- Poettible to name a precise date for our evacuation of the country. The Government, he said, were doing all in their power to replace European officials by natives, and two important offices—those of Postmaster-General and Harbour-Master at Alexandria—had been recently given te Emotians. Turning to the subject of the Debt, he tointeti out that Europeans were now taxed equally with uatives, which, he hoped, would ultimately result in a general alleviation of taxation, and he denied that nothing ..._WaS being done to reduce expenditure. On the con- rory, there had been a large reduction during the last 'WG years, eepecially in the expenditure for military Purposes. Or. Clark and Sir G. Balfour continued the debate, and opt Tanner spoke until a quarter to • six when, occording to the rules of the House, the debate stood adjourned. The House adjourned at 5 50 pm. .:11644.11 lamp eine HOUSE OF COMMONS.--Mdelltrt. t -I ~ • ethr The Speaker took the chair'at 3 50 p.m. Mr. Sertetee asked for leave to introduce a bill to es- tablish a Court of Appeal •in eritrenal cases. .. . QUESTIONS. . .. e . .„ Mr. STaNtropv, in reply to Mr. Hatibu7, ' said that at the end of last week there were at En eld 519 skilled artisans and 579 unskilled employed in the manufacture of rifles; 287 skilled and 100 unskilled were employed /caking swords and bayonets, 70 skilled and 60 unskilled Were occupied at machine work, and 158 skilled and 150 unskilled were engaged in other employment. Mr. BRYCE asked the Homo Secretary whether he was now in a position, having ascertained the facts relating to the recent arrest of Mdlle. Drouin in the Isle of Wight, to state what apology or coemensation .be proposed to Make to her tor the erave inconvenience and annoy- 'arlee she ha& suffered ?—Mr. Marrintws had stig- eated to the Chief Constable of Hampshire that e should offer Mdlle. Drouin ,a, full apology, and he would consult immediately with the Treasury els to a solatium in consideration of the, annoyance she hadsuffered. The hon. member was 'aware that this katter raised an international question. Mdlle. Drouin was a lady of perfect respectability and unimpeachable Character, and he greatly regretted that she bad suf- mired. He would add, however, that the Hampshire con- ,atabillary had no alternative, from) the information they had received, but to take the lady before the magistrate. Sir JAmas FERGUSSON rose to correct a mistake he had made on Saturday last. He had then stated the cost of the army of occupation in Egypt at £98,000, but he should have stated it at £200,000, the smaller sum lie had put it at being that to which the Government hoped to bring the cost.—Mr. BRYCE asked the Government to give some statement as to what was to be the policy in Egypt for the next six months. He also desired an explanation as to the intentions of the Government with regard to the French occupation of the New Hebrides. As late as last December a fresh batch of French convicts had been sent out to New Caledonia, and every additional batch created further alarm among the English colonists, He trusted the Government would give an assurance that they were not allowing the settlement of the New Hebrides and the Suez Canal question to depend one upon the other. (Hear, hear.) - Sir J. FERGUSSON, replying, assured the Committee that with regard to the occupation of Egypt her Majesty's Government were desirous of doing all they could to bring the country into a position in which they might safely withdraw the British Army. The French Government held that the protection of their subjects required the temporary occupation of the New Hebrides by a military force, but her Majesty's Government could not look without some fear and doubt on a continued occupation by a military force of a group of islands which it had been agreed between France and England should remain perfectly neutral. There certainly had been no connection admitted by her Majesty's Govern- ment between the questions of the New liebrides and of the neutralisation of the Suez Canal—(hear, hear)—but the Government had not objected to discuss the two questions at the same time. The question of the coloni- sation of the New Hebrides formed no part of the agree- ment between the two countries.

THE NATIONAL LEAGUE: MIL GLADSTONE'S MOTION.— Mr. GLADSTONE, who was greeted with cheers, thought it might be for the convenience of the House that he should state the terms of his address be proposed to submit to- morrow. They were : " That an address be presented to Her Majesty humbly to represent to Her Majesty that there has been laid before this House a special proclama- tion of the Viceroy of Ireland declaring the association known as the National League to be a dangerous associa- tion under the Criminal Law Procedure (Ireland) Act of 1887 ; that no information has been issued to Parliament to justify the issue of the said special proclamation by virtue of which Her Majesty's subjects are liable to be punished as criminals without judicial inquiry as to the nature of their case ; and that this House, in the absence of such in- formation, prays that the said proclamation may not con- tinue in force as to the association named and described therein."_ (Cheers.).

THE PROCLAMATION OF THE LEAGUE.

After the questions had been disposed of, it was agreed. on the motion of Mr. SMITH, to postpone the orders of the day until after the notice of motion relating to the special proclamation of the Irish National League. Mr. OtansTostn, who moved the address of which he had given notice, field an act of great importance and, as he thought, of great violence had been performed by the Ex- ecutive Government, which, according to the law of the land, Could tot be their act alone, for the action of Parlia- ment wag ke misential with respect to the proclamation of the National League as the action of the Executive itself. The proclamation declared that the National League pro- moted and incited to acts of violence and intimidation, and this conclusion must be founded on information. But where was the information? They had a title to know the grounds upon which the Govern- ment had arrived at this conclusion, and they claimed to he supplied with them. It the facts were with- held, then there were three propositions which the Opposi- Hod must urge upon the House and the Government. First, it was a slight, almost an outrage, upon the dignity of Par- liament to suppose it was to discharge a statutory duty of this importance without being in possession of the grounds upon which alone the discharge of that duty must depend ; seo°ndlY, it reduced to utter destruction the main conten- tions of the Government put forward when they were dis- cussing the Crimes Act. The safeguard then promised had preyed but a farce, and he wanted to know what was the value and meaning of Parliamentary approval given in the

div.p: • dark,blindfolded,and in ignoran2Oacte. That was the delu- sion practised on Parliament and the country. tithe Govern- ment had good cause to believe that the National League was responsible for the evils they pretended existed, why did they not suppress the organisation ? If the Govern- ment had had cause to proclaim the League, they would have asked Parliament to agree with them in the enact. ment of such a statute. Thirdly, he asked what the House was to think of information that they knew would not bear the light. He had always contended that the Government were legislating against combination apart from crime. Now was the time to show that he and his friends were wrong, but the Government shrank from the test and declined the challenge. The concurrence of Parliament was therefore reduced to a mere imposture. The Crimes Bill was a new form of suspending the Habeas Corpus Act, and the arbi- trary will of the Government had been substituted for the regular action of the law. This was a principle most dangerous and most disgraceful to be enacted in any country, but most of all in Ireland. His impression was that the action of the Government would substitute secret and clandestine action for action °pee and in the eye of day. Though much hardship must be involved in the action of popular combi- nation, was that a reason why the House should declare it was illegal ? If they struck at combination on the part of the masses they would deprive them of the only weapon which yet remained to them. Nobody had done anything for the tenants until the League was established, and when landlords could not let their farms they had been forced to consider the question of rent. By the course they were pursuing the Government departed from the ordinary pro- cesses of the law and became law breakers rather than law abiders, and thus set a dangerous example to the people of Ireland. Mr. A. J. BALFOUR said he would show that the National League was responsible for boycotting. The difficulty was not to obtain information, but to select it from the enormous mast of evidence which was in the bands of the Govern- ment. There was quite sufficient to found a case for the proclamation of the League, not in confidential reports, bid in the columns of the newspapers. The reason why the League had not been proclaimed before was because the Government wished for the Land Bill to become law before they proclaimed it. Nearly 5,000 persons in Ireland were at this moment under the curse of boycotting. The arguments the right hon. gentleman had used to defend boycotting might be used with equal force to defend assassination, and he ought to be careful when he defended that which he had once so strongly condemned. The unwritten law of the National League was supreme, and the people were in- timidated into supporting its programme. He allezed that the action of the League was not confined to land, but dis- turbed every relation of life. The debate was continued by Mr. E. Harrington, Lord Ebrington, Mr. Buchanan, Mr. T. W. THE BULOA.RIAN SITUATION.—RUSSIA'S LATEST MOVE: PROPOSED JOINTOCOU- PATION OF THE COUNTRY: CoNsTaxxisopue, Sardr/DAY.—Russio is doing her utmost to persuade the Porte to take active measures in Bulgaria. An extraordinary council of Ministers, under the presidency of the Sultan, took place on Thursday night. The question of granting Prince Ferdinand a fir- man as Governor-general of Eastern Rouniella was dis- cussed. The council was in its favour, and it is thought that upon satisfactory replies being received from the Powers to #' - Porte's note .Artin Effendi will be sent to , Bulgaria (v. • bearer of the firman. 1311175SELS, SUNDAY.—The Nerd continues to Speak con- temptuously of Prince-Ferdinand as a mere puppet of the ex-Regents. The St. Petersburg correspondent says the Powers ought to order Prince Ferdinand to leave Bulgaria. Turkey's future supremacy in the Otto- man Empire depends on her conduct on the present occasion. SOFIA, Surroar.—M. Radoslavoff is said to have declined the request of Prince Ferdinand that he should under- take the formation of a new Cabinet, and M. Tontcheff has also refused to attempt the task. It is feared that in the event of Austria following the example of Ger- many in breaking off the official relations with the .Government of Prince Ferninand the other Powers will adopt the same course. SOFIA, MONDAY—Great preparations have been made here for the reception of Prince Ferdinand, and much animation prevails throughout the town. Eight large triumphal arches have been erected bearing the inscrip- tions " Liberty" and "Independence." The whole popu- lation is on the move, and everyone seems determined to give the Prince a hearty welcome. According to the official programme, the Prince will arrive at half-past rive o'clock in the afternoon. The commander of the troops and the Prefect will meet him before he enters the town. On arriving a salute of artillery will be fired. The garrison of Sofia will take up its position to the right of the triumphal arch. The Mayor and members of the municipality will then welcome him and offer him bread and salt. The Prince will then proceed to the cathedral and receive the Bulgarian clergy. Unarmed soldiers will keep the line of route. On the way he will receive the Catholic clergy and the other religious bodies. The garrison of Sofia will defile before the palace. At night the whole town will be illuminated. Sr. ParEnsnuso, MoNDAy.—In political circles here it is to-day eensitered certain that the Porte will acquiesce • in Russia's proposition for a simultatieouS occupation of Bulgaria by Russian and Turkish troops. MOSCOW, MONDAY.—Tho Moscow Gazette states that Russia'aprotest agaiest Pence Ferdinand's election and arrival in Bulgaria ha.s.givpn great satisfaction through- out the country, and considers the Prince's retirement inevitable.
FRANCE. --- DUELLING. -- FOREST FIRE.

_ Pews, Sotsusv.—A duel, which resulted in serious con- sequences to both combatants, took place yesterday near Paris between M. Georges de Labruyere and M. de Mel- ville,l lieutenant of dragoons. The combat, which had its origin in aepersonal matter, was a brief one. It had continued for only a few minutes when M. de Melville, attacking with great vigour, drove the point of his sword right through his adversary, piercing the right lung. M. de Lahruyere returned the thrust instantly, and struck M. do Melville full in the breast. The sword came in contact with a rib and bent to a considerable extent, then escaped from the point of impact, straight- ened, and passed through the left lung. Both com- batants fell grievously wounded. M. de Labruyere was taken to an adjacent house, where he will remain for some time. M. de Melville insisted on being taken back to his own quarters In the barracks. Ptaus,MONDAY.—The forest do the picturesque moun- taM Carri, 20 miles from Marseilles, has been destroyed by fire. The scene presepted from the Corniche-road was maghificent. A storm raged at the same time as the fire, and no troops 'could be sent across by sea, the Mediterranean was sty rough. It is impossible to estimate the value of the woods which have been destroyed, but the loss must be very great.
IMPRISONMENT OF A PROTESTANT - • MISSIONARY.

, MADRID, SONDAY.—When the Spanish Government asserted its supremacy in 1885 over the Caroline Islands it promised the United States that it would respect the Protestant missions Wablished for more than 20 years in the principal islands of the group. The Spanish authori- ties have, nevertheless, arrested and imprisoned at Manilla since June Net, the Der. Edward Deane, aged 79, one of the earliest and most influential missionaries in the island of Ponape. The cause Of the arrest was the resistance he offered when the Spaniards interfered with the work of the missions after he had offered to pay the heavy taxies levied by the new rules, which had never appeared in Ponape before 1836. The American Govern- ment has made strong representations in order to obtain the release of the missionary.

_ JONPESSI. ON. A remarkable circurnstane,e in connection with the Lipski case occurred on Sunday afterhoon, the prisoner having made a full confession a/ the crime to the Rev. S. Singer. The confession was in the following terms : " I, Israel Lipski, before appearing before God in judg- ment, desire to speak the whole truth concerning the crime of which lam accused. I will not die with a lie on my lips. I will not let others suffer eVen on suspicion for my sin. I alone was guilty of the murder of Miriam Angell.. I thought the woman had money in her room, so I entered, the door being unlocked and the woman asleep. I had no thought of violating her and I swear I never ap- proachod her with that object, nor did I wrong her in this way. Miriam Angell awoke before I could search for money, and cried out, but very • softly Thereupon I struck her on the head, and seized her by the neck and closed her mouth with my hand, so that she should not arouse the attention of those who were about the house. I had long been tired of my life, and had bought a pemy.wctrth of aquafortis that morning for the purPose O ptitting an end to myself. Suddenly I thought of the bottle I bad Au my pocket, and drew it out and poured some of the contents clown her throat. She fainted, and recognising my desperate condition I took the rest. The bottle was an old one, which I had formerly used, and was the same as that which I had taken with me to the oil shop. The quan- tity of aquafortis I took had no effect on me. Having an idea of people coming upstairs I crawled under the bed. The woman seemed already dead. There was only a short time from the moment, of my entering the room until I was taken away. In the agitation I also fainted. I do not know how it was my arms _became abrased. did not feel it, and was not aware of it. As to the door being locked on the inside, I myself did this immediately after I entered the room, wishing not to be interrupted. I solemnly declare that Rosenbloom and Schmuss know nothing whatever of the crime of which I have been guiltY, and I alone. I implore them to pardon me for having in my 'despair tried to cast the crime upon them. I also beseech the forgiveness of the bereaved husband. 'I admit that I have had a fair trial, and acknowledge Hie justice of the sentence that has been passed upon me. I desire to thank Mr. Hayward for hisefforts on my behalf, as well as all those who have interested themselves in me during this unhappy tamp. This confession is made of my own free will, and Is written down by Mr. Singer at my reqtest. May God comfort my loving father 'and mother, and may He accep4 my repentance and my death as an atonement for all my sins.—Sunday, August 21st, 1887. "(Signed) ISIIAXL Lima. "Witnesses :--S. Singer, minister; E. L. dfilmaas Governor of Her Majesty's Prison, Newgate." This statement was at once forwarded to the HOMO Secretary.

THE EXAM.INER. SATURDAY; A UGUS r - MR. H. M. S4TANLEY.-1- rTEitiS F THE EXPLORER. Sir Francis de 'Winton .hrisillE4,eived two letters from Mr. Stanley, one dated Mayiplst, and the other June 19th. These letters, Sir Frt.is states, prove that the rumour regarding Mr. Staehty s death cannot be true, since he sent the latest newp oI himself ti. 4 the Congo that could by any possibility reach Europe, and that it is an impossibility for any" news to come from the Aruwimi, across Africa, to Zanzibar, within the time specified. Mr. Stanley's first letter wr- written 547 miles above Leopoldville, and 892 from the Atlantic. There were with him then 640 men, 500 loads of goods, and some live stock. "Since leaving Rolobo (Mr. Stanley wrios) we have had no accident or incident worth mentionine —no losses in men or goods, no famine. no Inconveni- ence, no cause of anxiety. The net; .es welcomif in 4 everywhere, and sell us such abundance of food thatAitw people have already forgotten the pinching scantinlsf, the horrid meagreness, of their fare from the sea to the Pool. I suppose each man in the expedition has in- creased from 10 to 20 pounds in weight. The only fear I have now is that they will endanger the steamers by this remarkable increase in body." In the second letter, which is dated from the camp at Yambuga Rapids, Aruwimi Run, Mr. Stanley says they arrived there eight days behind the estimated time. He proceeds— "We captured this village by means of steamer whistles, which made such a hideous clamour that it served as a protection for the assaulting parties. We had talked for three hours. Time was passing away. The natives were obdurate, and putting themselves in the Achilles mariner, with poised spears and erected shields. The 7.anzibarees, arriving at the top, 80 feet high above river, found themselves in quite an empty village. The night's grace we had given them had enabled the natives to clear out their valuables. Poor souls! We did not need them without a price. Every fowl and goat had vanished, but we have got a square mile of cassava gar- dens to feed our garrison. The huts are or a narrow diameter, of the candle-extinguisher type, ranged in two rows on either side of a street, twenty feet wide. There are 194 huts in this village, just enough to house the advance force comfortably. Below and above us are miles of smaller villages, 15, 20, and 30 huts in each, a background of dense bush, front. being the 80-foot bluff rising above river. Some natives have come in; our 'scouts arrested about a dozen yester- day. They were all released with presents. It appears to me as though this country was the resort of all the fragments of tribes for many degrees around. I hear of over a dozen tribes being represented in as many miles here. The more people, the more food, of cotitte. We release our captives at once 'with small gifts and good words—seedlings, I hope, of a future amicab'e inter- course. If Barttelot will exercise patience with them, long before we return they will be a prosperous commu- nity, and friendship will be firmly established. While this letter is on its way to you I wonder what is in store for us. The Giver of all good things be with you always, and may He bless us both." Sir F. de.Winton, in his letter, says there now remains about 400 miles between Emin Pasha and the expedition. During part of this journey the natives may show some hostility; but, as we learn from Mr. Stanley's letters, they appear to be broken remnants of many tribe:, and their opposition, being that of small communities, with- out any unity of action, will be very trivial. Then, also, the couriers sent from the East Coast last March have brought to Emin the news of the despatch of the expedition and its probable route, and he doubtless will despatch a force to open up communication in the direction of the coming supplies. Let us suppose that Mr. Stanley left his camp at Yambuya about the 23rd of June, he would, with a selected caravan (his men well.. rested, well fed, and strong), reach the Albert Nyanza in 30 days ; and at this moment he and Emin are atm Wailelai arranging future plans, having despatched a,l caravan to the Aruwimi to bring up the remainder of the' supplies. A courier sent from Wadelai at the end of July would reach the coast the beginning or middle of October; about that date we may expect more news of the expedition. 'TAW

The Welshmen /of Manchester have opened a defence fund on behalf of the 31 men charged with rioting at Llangwm. Henry lSlc.Grattom, residing in Buchanan-street, Coatbridge, was arrested on Monday morning, charged with the culpable homicide of Edward Lnnie, iron roller, by striking him on the face last Monday, causing CODEMB.• 11 of the brain. On Saturday morning three little boys were chasing butterflies in a field near Westhoughton, when one of them, aged eight, named John Hodkinson, tumbled over a rail into a pool of water six feet deep, and was diowned. Thelbody was recovered 15 minutes afterwards. ROBBING A CEMETERY. —At Jarrow Police Court, on Monday, James Dixon, a respectably dressed man, was charged witYstealing two glass shades from graves in Jarrow Cemetery. It was stated that eight shades had been stolen. The prisoner was committed for trial at the Quarter Sessions. TRADE Rim NEAR BIRMINGRAM.—The strike in the Bir- mingham nail trade has resulted in another serious dis- turbance. A party of about 20 strikers went out in a brake to Brohmgrove, where therencountered a number of men who were put on in place of the old hands. A desperate fight followed. The men sustained dangerous injuries, and several sustained minor injuries. A num- ber of bystanders were badly hurt with missiles.

A salmon 8741 b. in weight was exposed for sale in the Central Fish Market, Farringdon-road, London, on Saturday. It was a male fish, or what is known in the North of England among fishermen as an "eke." No scales were on it, and it was turning somewhat brown or copper-coloured. There was an indentation on the tail part just beyond the umbilical fin, which showed that it had been gaffed or leistered. It was taken in the river Tay, on Mr. Dunn's estate. A RACE ROOND THE ISLE OF MAN.—The steamers the Lancashire Witch, belonging to the Lancashire line, the Ben-my-Chree, of the Old Manx line, and the Manx Queen, belonging to the Barrow Company., have had a race round the island. The Lancashire Witch made the voyage in half an hour less‘than her oppenents. The time was :—Manx Queen sailM at 10 5, Ben-my-Chree at 10 30, Lancashire Witch at 10 45. The Lancashire Witch arrived at 3, the Manx Queen at 3 4, and the Ben-my. Chree at 3 25.

CA.PTIIRE OF A COINEII--Two Liverpool policemen On Saturday night made a capture of a base owner. They had gone to a suspected house in Gilt-street, and arrested a woman who called out for "Ned." One of the officers at once went upstairs, and was confronted by a power- ful middle-aged man, who was surrounded by all the implements for coining. A desperate struggle ensued, but the man was secured, and carried away with all his apparatus and a number of base florins. He was brought before the magistrates on Monday, and remanded for a week. , Tug Tints AGITATION.—The Bishop of Bangor in the course of his triennial charge on Monday referred to the anti-tithe agitation in his diocese, remarking that the prime movers were men who had very small interest in the matter, and were in no wise affected by the depressed 4tate of agriculture, but were taking advantage of the ,depression to push forward the question of Disestablish- , ment. The right rev, prelate suggested that until legis- lation placed the matter upon a satisfactory footing the clergy should organise to enforce their just andlegal claims.

ACCIDENT IN KEYHAM DOCXYARD.—A work, man named John Keiley was the victim of a terrible accident on Monday afternoon in the boiler shop of Keyham Dockyard, Plymouth. He was superintending the work of an overhead travelling crane, when his clothes became entangled in the machinery, and he was drawn up and dashed against the sharp edge of the iron platform with such tremendous force that his head and one of his arms were completely severed from his body, and fell at the feet of the workmen below. div.head: 711 E __SERIOUS FISHING AFFRAY AT OSTEND.
div.p: 711 E __SERIOUS FISHING AFFRAY AT OSTEND.

THE HAGUE, WEDNESDAY MONT.—The rioting at Ostend broke out afresh to-day, and the Civic Guards had to be called out to assist in the suppression of the disturbances. A number of Belgian fishermen had boarded two English fishing smacks and were preventing the crew from dis- charging their cargo, when the Guards came up and had to fire on the rioters. Three men have already died, and five snore are seriously wounded. This afternoon a body of regular troops arrived in Ostend from Bruges. The town is in a state of great azitation, and the situation is regarded as Very serious.

On Saturday the Conservative members received a circular letter from Mr. W. H. Smith, expressing his great regret at being compelled to ask honourable members to forego their holidays at so late a period of the session. But events render it necereary that the Government should be strongly supported at the present , juncture, and, therefore, every member of the party is i earnestly requested to attend in his place during the pre- I lent week. Those members who have not paired are; asked on no account to do so until further notice. Mr. Smith's letter is considered to be one of the strongest Ministerial whips issued for a number of years. Sin W. ilanCOnwr AT RELDING.—Sir Wm. Harcourt, speaking at Reading on Wednesday night, twitted Mr. Chamberlain and the Liberal Unionists with their inconsis- tency. They had refused to support moderate coercion Coupled with local government, and now had passed a severe measure which was hateful to the country, with nethine in the way of reel land reform or local government. They were gradually losiric support throughout the country, as the elections showed, and Mr. Russell, who had stumped the country for the Unionists, and had been trotted out by Lord Salisbury at Carlton, had been obliged to leave the party, and declared that Ulster was now given over to Par- nellites. He did not, however, object to that, for it Was I another step towards Home Rule. re-/ THE NATIONAL LEAGUE PROCLAMATION. ' A great pepular demonstration against the proclamation of the National League took place on Tuesday night in Dublin, where three crowded meetings were, addressed by prominent English and Irish Home Rule members of Par- liament. At the principal gathering, in the Rotondo. the 1 I Lord Mayor of Dublin presided, and said his fellow citizens I cared nothing for what might come from the Castle, and they despised and defied the proclamation. The League I had been described by the Government as a "dangerous association," but he averred that it was only dangerous to 1 rack-renters, tyrants, and oppressors. On the motion of Professor Galbraith, seconded by Mr. Scully, and supported amongst others by Mr Jacob Bright, M.P., and Mr Cobb, M.P., 1 a resolution was adopted denouncing the proclamation as an unscrupulous attempt to drive the Irish people from the path of peaceful and constitutional agitation, and to disarm I them of the organisation which had suppressed crime ' and outrage. The proceedings throughout were most en- 1 thnsiastic. I MR. BRADLAUGH, M.P., ON THE LIBERAL UNIONISTS. On Sunday, at Liverpool, Mr. Bradlaugh, speaking of 1 the Liberal Unionists, said they had lost their secretary, Mr. Maude, one of the most loyal of men, whose seces- sion justified him in saying that the crevices inside the Union were larger than they saw from the outside. Sir George Trevelyan had left it; so had Mr. T. W. Russell, who was no feather-bed soldier; and Mr. Chamberlain had lately been sitting on a rail. He had lately wriggled, and one leg was much nearer the ground than the other: but he would not prophesy which side of him would go over first, notwithstanding his Ironclad declaration at the beginning of the session that he would give no vote which would throw out of office the present Gavernment. There was an old saying that rats always deserted a sinking ship, and it was no wonder some of the two- legged or four-legged creatures now sought safety on the shore. This party, which rose into existence a few months ago, would in a few weeks be dead and buried, for the electors had declared against the Liberal Union- ists. He denounced Mr. Chamberlain, who had joined Mr. Gladstone's last Administration with a full know- ledge of the reasons why Lord Hartington held aloof from it. If Mr. Chamberlain deemed it right to break with Mr. Gladstone not on the matter of principle, but of detail and method, was at least his duty to speak re- spectfully of the leader he had quitted. As to the future, there would soon be only two distinct parties—the party of the aristocracy and the party of labour and manufac- turing industry. , THE LIBERALITNIONIST SPLIT. V Mr. E. W. Maude, who has resigned the post of secre- tary of the Liberal Union and vice-president of the National Radical Union, has promised to take an early opportunity after his return from Germany to make a public statement of the reasons which have induced him to take this step. Being a vice-president of the Liberal League, Mr. Maude has determined, with the approval of the executive council, to make this statement at the demonstration which the League, supported by other kindred ossociations, are proposing to hold at the Alexandra Palace on the §th of September. In a letter dated from the Hotel Victoria, Kissingen, 'Bavaria, the 17th instant, Mr. Maude says:—" My position at present is a peculiar one, as I have severed my official and private connection with tijp Liberal Unionist party, in consequence of the irrereencilsble ' attitude assumed by its chiefs towards the Liberal party, end their apparent intention of ignoring the considerable concessions made by Mr. Gladstone to remove the objec- tions entertained by many strong Radicals to his Irish bills of last ygar. I believe my explanation will incluse many Radical Unionists to follow my example and re- turn to the Liberal fokl. I should not presume to sug- gest this if 1_44 DAfeel the necessity of pointing out to • 'rgiif strong Radicals the futility of gadical Unionism now that Mr. Gladstone has, met most of the objections ' they raised to his Irish bills last year." The Irish Times gives the text of a letter from Mr. T. W. Russell, M.P., which the hon.gehtlemain wrote on Friday in reply to an inquiry. It is as follows: "After carefully considering Thursday night's .proceedings, which, in my opinion, handed aver the prom of Ulster to Mr. Parnell, I communicated my resignati to the ck Liberal Unionist whips on Satin-day, and cance all the platform work I had undertaken for the winter. In-my opinion, the action of the Government and the majority 1 of the Liberal Unionist party has gravely complicated the Irish problem, and I cannot consent to share the re- sponsibility in any shape or form. I only desire to add that my secession does not involve a vote for Home Rule. It is the only protest I can make against a policy the Consequences of which I very much dread." A duplicate of Mr. Russell's letter is said to have been sent by Mr. T. Lee, who also withdraws from the Liberal . UnTranst party. Lord Hal tington, writing to Mr. T. W. Russell, expresses his regret that the hon, member has found it necessary to take the course he has done in withdrawing from the Liberal Unionist organisation, and desires to meet him and talk the matter over with him. Mr. Russell has replied that he is as much a Liberal Unionist as ever, but that he has a diffi- cult position to fill, and under the circumstances he feels that he must work outside the organisation instead of within it.

MR. CHAMBERLAIN AT BIRMINGHAM. Speaking in his own grounds, near Birmingham, on Sat- urday afternoon, to the members of the National Radical Union, Mr J.Chamberlain, M.P., said that he and those who acted with him were precluded from blaming the Govern- ment severely for using the powers they had so recently teen given. Personally he regretted the action the Govern- ment I3ad taken in proclaiming the Land League, as he held that no emergency had arisen which called for such a step. While admitting that the Government had a tight to disre- gard the advice of the Liberal Unionists,he said that he and his colleagues who had given that advice would con- Own to occupy the attitude of independent friends of the Governrnent,and that when they differed from the Govern- ment they would express their difference in the usual way by their votes if the action of the Government was chal- lenged in the lions') of Commons. He denied absolutely the rumour that he bad reined his connection with the Liberal Unionist party, and remarked that although it was ' true he differed from the Government on this one point, he was prepared to support their general policy so far as. in his judgment, it tended towards the maintenance of the Union, and declared that he had seen no reason why any , Liberal Unionist should desert the party with which be had connected himself, or the leader, Lord Hartington, Who had up to the present led them with conspicuous ability and loyalty. Referring to the recent elections, Mr Chamberlain expressed the *pinion that the Gladstonian candidates had Increased their vote by throwing overboard altogether the policy of Mr Gladstone. While his followers did this, Mr Gladstone himself was so vague that his statements were liable to be interpreted in two ways. Consequently, if ho , was again returned to power he would be entirely unpledged, and he (Mr Chamberlain) did not believe the" repentant sinners" would be able again to leave the party should Mr Gladstone revert to his old policy.

were competing for the Horsleydown prize skiff, taking place in the vicinity of Ray's Wharf, Hors, down, about a nails below London Bridge,sand thevarioiss preliminary heats having been decided, the final one *air in progress. Among the numerous spectators of the race were a group of 35 people, who secured an advan- tageous point of view by clambering upon a hay-laden barge which was lying in the river. In the excitement produced by the deciding heat of the contest these people all rushed to the port side of the barge, which in conse- quence heeled over and precipitated all ite occupants save one into the water at a time when there were no other• 'boats within convenient distance. One version of the sad affair is, that the hay fell on the top of some of the ' people, knocking them into the water, and prevented them from being seen or heard. At all events, delay necessarily occurred before succour could be brought, and when it did arrive several persons had sunk never to rise again alive. Some of the men being expert swimmers made for the shore, and others managed to keep themselves afloat until assistance arrived in the shape of the steam launch, James Yates, belonging to ' Mr. B. Murphy, and of a number of watermen's boats which rescued them from their peril. The only nee- who was not precipitated from the barge w- Crawley, a waterman, who afterwards - work of rescue. He believes that Re lost, and his estimate is borne out by' the accident. Later particulars show that the . the loss of life made in some greatly exaggerated. Several lives,' been fost. The barge belongs to Mr. of Fobbing, Essex, and was moored at accident about thirty yards from the ed about three-quarters of a mile below Lee was very near low water when a numb( bered on board to witness the regatta, still running out As the bank of the is thickly covered with Mud, and erably, the inshore side of the into contact with the mud-bank, wards the river after rebounding from About a hundred trusses of hay were stacked on the barge, and the weight of the men and boys on the top of these caused some of the trusses to slip, and precipitated' those standing on the outer edge of the barge into the ,river. The owner of the barge had previously warned those on board of their dangerous position. Fourteen er fifteen persons were thrown into the water, which was not more than five feet deep. The greatest number of these,hovvever, were rescued by boats, or saved them- selves lay clinging to floating trusses, and then clamber- ing on board the barge. In addition to Jeremiah O'Brien, whose body was recovered shortly after the accident, the Thames police after dragging the place all night, succeeded early yesterday in recovering two more bodies. Shortly after eleven o'clock a fourth body was recovered from the mud. The police arissill dragging the river. AMATEUR AGREEMENTS AT RUZI- . DORN. THE HIRING SYSTEM. ' At Runcorn County Court, on Tuesday, before his Honour Judge Ffoulkes. Messrs Claff and Company, furniture dealers, Runcorn and Widnes. brought an action against James Jolley, tinsmith, Bridge-street, to recover £5 fos. The summons was in the follow- ing terms: " The plaintiffs demand of you the de- livery of the following articles, hired from them by William Shaw, of Granville-street, and unlawfully sold by him to you :—One chest drawers £4 los, and the sum of £1 for their detention."—air Rides!, of Warring- ton, appeared for the plaintiffs, and stated that on the 21st February of the present year, William Shaw, who was son- in-law to the defendant, hired from the plaintiff a chest of drawers worth £4 10s, and he signed an agreement to pay that amount. Shaw made about 15 payments, amounting to upwards of £l, but after the I lth July be made default in his payments, and the plaintiffs ascertained that Shaw had left his residence and sold the drawers to the defend- ant. The plaintiffs' representative demanded the article, but the defendant said be had paid for tie drawers and would stick to them. He need not tell his Honour that a man who had no right in goodl could not by making a sale transfer any right to another person.—Emmanuel Blank, of Ellesmere-street, manager of the Runcorn branch of Messrs Claffa' business, proved the agreement, which was given in.—His Honour pointed out that the agreement stated " The hirer having paid to the owner the sum of £4 10s 01 (and for which sum cre- dit is not to be given on account of rent unless and until the purchase is effected hereinafter men- tioned)." According to that the plaintiffs had received full value of the drawers.—The witness said he filled up the agreement, but he had not received the money. His Honour : I cannot let him contradict his written statement. —Mr. Rideal contended that the fact that Sbaw had paid 15 instalments after the signing of that agreement was strong corroboration of the witness's statement that there was an error in the agreement. —Abraham Claff having given evidence, His Honour said the -agreement clearly stated the money was paid. Therefore the drawers had be- come the property of Shaw, and he gave a verdict for the defend/int.—An action was then bronght by Messrs. Claff and Company against Luke Holmes, auctioneer, High-street, L Ruveorn.—Mr. &deal said this Case was somewhat different to the last one, but he was bound to tell His Honour that the hiring agreement under which the plaintiffs reed Was filled up in precisely the sarne way that I the former agreem.nt was. If the hirer bad at the time of signing the agreement paid the whole of the purchase falooey then it was quits evident by a common sense con- struction of the terms that taking the contract as a whole, there would be no necessity for any future payments. In this case John Gough hired 6 chairs one dresser, and a pair of mattresses, and after the date of the agreements no has than 20 payments were made. If the agree- ment was to he constructed literally then Gough had made the plaintiffs a present of those 20 payments. It appeared that Goegh was a respectable boatman. During Gongls'a absence from home his wife sold the whole of the furniture, amongst which were the articles hired from the plaintiffs, to the defendant Holmes for the sum of 245. The wife was Convicted of robbery, and was sentenced to a month's lin- prisonment. As soon as ever the goods had got into the possession of the defendant Emmanuel Blank went and told him the articles were hired, and that Mrs Gough had no power to sell them. Notwithstanding this he sold the goods, but he bad since then offered to return one portion of furniture.—Emmannel Blank deposed that the manner in which the agreement was filled up was a mistake. Gcugh had made 20 payments towards the value of the goods.— His Honour said the argesMent put the plaintiffs out of court notwithstanding they said they had not received the actual purchase money for these things.—Judgment was given for the defendant, with costs.

. . The late Mrs. Evans, widow of the late Admiral Geo. Evans, has bv her will, which has just been proved, be- queathed £3SG to the Royal National Lifeboat _lnstitu- tion for a lifeboat to be called the George Evans, to be stationed at Liverpool, or some other part of the river Mersey. Admiral Evans, whose name will thus be com- memorated on the river, was for 34 years conservator of the Mersey. An inquest was held at Derby on Saturday, on the bodies Of Alfred Ling and his three children, supposed to have been drowned by the former in the canal. The police produced a note found in the man's pocket, accusing some of his fellow-strikers of being traitors, and charg- ing them and the Midland Railway Company with being the cause of his misfortunes. The note added, "May God forgive me for this rash act." An open verdict was returned. _ . _

BRADLATICIII.—Mr. Cham- berlain having stated that he should vote against the Gov- ernment for the proclamation of the National League, a correspondent drew his attention to the statement of Mr. Bradlaugh at Liverpool. on Sunday, that Mr. Chamberlain declared early in the session that he would give no vote that would throw out the Government. Mr. Chamberlain wrote on Tbursdoy morning that he sees no reason for Viking any notice of Mr. Bradlangh's speech, and he says he has nothing to add to what be said on Saturday last.

Our readers will have observed that for 'everal weeks there has been an interesting Correspondence in our columns on the tern- terance question. The annual Brewster essions are now being held throughout the ,rAtritry, and in view of applicalions for new ficenses in this district the time is opportune Or Passing under review the drinking habits t)4 SOCiety, and the general effect of alcohol ;11 the human system. In another column 'here will be found a lengthy communication .rorn our old and valued. contributor, "Clif- f°rd Dix," He is pretty free in his criticism or teetotallers, and, as he has a good deal to 84)1 in favour of the use of alcohol in moder- re quantities, we propose to traverse his etter in order to show that what he has been setting up in the way of evidence is little better than a house of cards. Our cot- respondent begins by quoting Sir WILLIAM 4.,CSBERTS as stating that malt liquors, pro- ,,ided th.ry are sound and free from acidity. l_ntelfere little with salivary digestion. But it is no great merit in a thing to say r°t under certain piescribed conditions it , es but little harm. As to light beer, when t;Yrell up," being favourable to stomach tOestion, we cannot but remark that even tllB is a very guarded opinion: and further, at it is in conflict with the opinion of tVestigators whose authority is greater than V4t of the Manchester baronet. Sir HENRY 110MPSON is referred to as though he were tti:favourable to teetotalism ; but in a letter tn the ARCFIBISHOP OF CANTERBURY, he 1/41.1 have long had the conviction that there is no e4ater cause of evil, moral and physical, in the %Orr/ than the use of alcoholic beverages. I do I)toPean by this that extreme indulgence which tices drunkenness. The habitual use of fer- t4letel liquors to an extent far short of what is thlitBBary to produce that condition, and such as is Ik4 e common in all ranks of society, injures the ltti and diminishes the mental power to an ex- it „'which I think few people are aware of. Such, kor",s'l events, is the result of observation during than twenty years of professional life de- e' hospital practice, and to private practice 'Per rank above it. Thus, I have no hesitation tltributing a very large proportion of some of totn"Qost painful and dangerous maladies which Iznder my notice, as well as those which 'Si Medical man has to treat, to the ordinary and of fermented drink, taken in the quantity l'hie" is conventionally deemed moderate. 111 41 We should say. is a fair set off as against lk(),lse of the "light beer" of Sir WILLIAM tip)? 11:rs, who requires that it shall be "well , before it is well down. as Clifford Dix" next quotes the " Times " i‘ an authority in favour of the use of tarsic°hol as an element of diet ;" and we hardly help suspecting that he is poking at Our readers ; for he does not need to told pc,tl d that the fact that the " Times " op- tht et a movement which has for its object benefit 01 the people is about the 110 evidence that can be afforded that those tt B,4PPort that movement are in the right. eAve taking the "Times " on its merits, we 1444 to say that it strikes blindly at the re- Nos °I. the most careful observation, and the N,t` ,scientific experiments, when it asserts that is "a highly economical force," 'oat its moderate use is conducive to ex- and vigour " for all engaged in brain qtA, or in physical work of an arduous SBacter, particularly such as requires quick- Rat iltnd concentration." To begin with the 411kts.latement, it is not only not true, but, as ,vprae would say, "it is curiously the re- the truth." There is nothing in which Ilitiree,,4oess and concentration "are more re- n•-‘4 than in games and sports; but—and 1)1)1Lic/te CaG•sell's " Book of Health," while th e to ordinary observation—' it is found tr Ven slight alcoholic indulgence greatly th cest e chances of success. n them at& is , A 'Riau Competitors] it is necessary that co - th °ll should be as perfect as possible, effect of alcohol iq to lessen co- -I;s,hit is DilernPorarily uhn a single dose t V'en it .at'etl, and to affo...z it permanently 41°' is re' I , indulged • " It • Wri ou.ar 5 in. is well "hat some of the best shots at Wim-

I bledon are abstainers; bet, apart from that, what would be thought of the marksman run- ning up for the Queen's Prize who, prior to taking his last shot, partook of a glass of light beer "well up," believing, as the "Times" has it, that it was conducive to "quickness and concentration." Would he not be condemned for running such a risk: and, if he failed, would he not be spoken of as a fool for thus spoiling his chance ? As to resorting to the use of alcohol in cases of brain work—it is akin to madness. It is one way, to use a homely phrase, of burning the candle at both ends, and sometimes leads to insanity. Out of sxi cases admitted into the West Riding Asylum in one year, 17.79 per cent were due either to intemperance, or to the use of alcohol when there was a ten- dency to insanity. Alcohol does not strengthen the brain ; it weakens it; and it is just as useless in case of" physical work of an ardu- ous character." In the tenth volume of " Health Lectures for the People," just pub- lished by Mr. JOHN HEYWOOD, we find the following pertinent passage in the lecture by Dr. RANSOME on "Some Causes of Preventa- ble Diseases ": "Science has proved conclusively that alcohol is sedative in its action upon the sympathetic nervous system, and that it diminshes the molecular changes and therefore energy in the body; and a large experience in campaigns in Arctic voyages, and in the exploration of the torrid regions of the globe, has amply shown that work is better per- formed without alcohol than with it." Our correspondent tells us that Professor LEONE LEVI has shown conclusively that it is not true to assert that drunkenness and crime go hand in band. There is surely some mistake here; Professor LEVI cannot have shown anything conclusively which is contrary to the common experience of man- kind. In the standard lecture we have just quoted, Dr. RANSOME says :—" With regard to crime, the testimony of judges, magis- trates, and governors of gaols is over-whelm- ing as to the results of intemperance. In the answers to a committee of the Houses of Convocation relating to the subject, there was a general consent amongst those gentle- men that about three-fourths of the crimes of violence brought into the various courts were due directly or indirectly to the agency of drink." We might go on to show that "strong drink" has a great deal to do with filling our workhouses as well as our prisons and lunatic asylumns ; or proceed to demon- strate by statistics which cannot be shaken that .the teetotaller has better health and lives longer than even the moderate drinker ; but we shall have other opportunities of dealing with these important features of the drink question. We agree with "CLIFFORD Dix" in looking to education and sanitation as aids to temperance; but we are entirely opposed to him in thinking that it is desir- able that "there should be less interference with the publicans." There is an enforcement of the law which provides that the offender who is drunk and disorderly shall be punished; but from some cause or other we hear little of the provision for punishing the landlord who makes him drunk. Publicans require to be more interfered with in that and in other respects. The more they are tied down and the less mischief they will do. It is axiomatic to say that drunkenness in- creases with the increase of the facilities for drinking; and it is to be hoped that the Licensing Committee, on Monday, will, for their own credit and the credit of the town, dismiss the applications for new licenses which will come before them. It is desir- able in the interests of the inhabitants that there should be a decrease rather than an increase in the number of licensed houses, not only in Warrinoton, but in almost every other town in the United Kingdom.

MR. CHAMBERLAIN does not appear to be in a very happy frame of mind just at present; and he is obviously a long way from success in the establishment of that National Party of which he is to be the leader. He broke away from Mr. GLADSTONE ; and, judging from the speech he made on Saturday, it would seem that he is now drifting apart from Lord HARTINGTON He still professes to acknowledge Lord HARTINGTON as his leader; but it is a leadership that has not much hold upon him, for, while his lordship is prepared to support the Tories in proclaiming the National League, Mr. CHAAIBERLAIN takes the trouble to state beforehand that he is opposed to this feature of their policy and will vote against it. He is in the curious position of nominally supporting the Government and following Lord HARTING- TON, and of actually being ready to' oppose the one and turn aside from the other. He tries to let the Tories down easy by saying that in proclaiming the National League he cannot, in "strong language," condemn their action; but they will not thank him for his soft word when he endangers the existence of the Government by giving a hard vote against them. According to Mr. CHAMBER- LAIN, it is an open secret that Lord HARTING- TON is like himself in being opposed to the proclamation of the League; but if Lord HARTINGTON were to express his disapproval by his vote, as Mr. CHAMBERLAIN proposes to do, the Government would be snuffed out. What a delightful situation for "the leaders of the Liberal Unionists ! " But it is just a little peculiar—not to say puzzling. Are we to infer that Lord HARIINGTON cannot afford to carry a conscience, since he cannot, like Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, give a vote in accord with his opinions? Or is it that the member for West Birmingham is to be blamed for posing as a follower who doesn't follow? Or, t,) hazard another supposition, can it be that Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S personal following has be- come so beautifully less that it is of no moment to anybody how he votes? An ex- planation of some kind is wanting, for his present relationship to the Tories, the Liberal Unionists, and the Liberals is simply be- wildering. With regard to the Coercion Act, it is something gained to find the member for West Birmingham admitting that it con- tains one "stringent provision," namely, that which "enables authorities in Ireland to bring before a stipendiary magistrate any person ac- cused of boycotting or of the other offences described in the act, and if he is found guilty to give him any punishment up to six months imprisonment with hard labour." Stringent indeed; and it is great shame that boycotting in Ireland should be punished with six months of hard labour, while in North Hunts members of the Primrose League are permitted. to boycott with impunity. Another significant admission which Mr. CHAMBERLAIN makes is that Ireland is "con- spicuously free from ordinary crime." He gives this as his reason for protesting against the proclamation of the National League. The reason is a sound one, but it is a pity Mr. CHAMBERLAIN did not think of it sooner. Ireland was "conspicuously free from serious crime" when the Coercion Bill was being forced through the House of Commons, and if MI. CHAMBERLAIN had done his duty as one who "hates coercion," he would have op.

He deserted Mr. GLADSTONE to support the Tories and follow Lord HAR- TINGTON, but at present he can neither follow his leader nor vote for the Tories. Between sundry stools he is coming to the ground. To lie there a while will do him 110 harm. It will help him, perhaps, to see the error of his ways, and in due time fit him to return to his place in the ranks of the Liberal party.
