The Local Board have provided a cemetery, and three mortuary chapels ; but as they decline to consecrate—which in- volves the appointment of a paid chaplin— the vicar refuses to bury or to allow any brother clergyman to bury in the new ground. Under present circumstances, a layman has to be called in, or a Nonconformist Minis- ter. After a while, if the vicar will only be good enough to keep up the strike against burials, the inhabitants will find that they can do just as well without him, and they will "go in" for disestablishment.
I.OCAL NEWS.

A WIDNES ARTIST.—Mr. W. Sadler, son of Mr. T. Sadler, builder, Widnes, has been awarded a silver medal in the national competition for model of figure from the antique. FIRE AT RUNCORN SOAP AND ALKALI COMPANY'S WORKS. —Late on 'Thursday night a fire was discovered to bevel broken out on the premises of the Runcorn Soap and Al- kali Company. Fortunately the works are well provided with tire appliances, and before the arrival of the fire brigade the flames had been entirely subdued. TRESPASSING ON TIM RAILWAY AT HALEBANE. -- At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Teuraday, Levi Hornby, a labourer, pleaded guilty to having, on the 28th July, tres- passed on the Sheffield and Midland Railway at Halebank. Vi'httelock appeared for the company, and stated they had determine I to put an end to these offence., which were very frt quent and a great nuisance. A sne of 5a and costs was iMpueed.. ASSAULT WITH A POKER AT RUNCORN.—Before Captain Hazlehurst, at Runcorn Police Court, on Tuesday, Eliza- beth Peacock, a single woman, who lived in Cooper-street, Wil4 brought up on remand charged with having on Tues- day, the 16th inst., feloniously wounded Jane Ball. a neigh- bour. by striking her on the head with a poker. The prose- cutor was again unable to appear, and the prisoner was remanded for a week. " PROFESSIONAL MUSICIAN" IN TROT/BLE AT Rust- conti.—Yesterday, at Runcorn Police Court, Philip Pan. nett, 17 years of age, was charged with having, on the pre- vious day travelled from Edge Hill to Runcorn without having previously paid his fare. As the prisoner was in possession of a hag containing a large number of articles which he could not satisfactorily account for he was re- manded until Monday. A FLATMAN DROWNED AT WIDNES.--Yeiterday afternoon the dead body of Richard Aaton, captain of the sailing flat Prima Donna, of Winsford, was taken from Widnes Dock. On Thursday night deceased left the .Swan Inn in company with Joseph Warburton a stevedore, who saw him safely on board his flat. At 4-30 a.m. yesterday moraine, Peter Har- rison. a duck porter, saw Aaton's cap on the deck of the fiat, but Aston himself could not be found. His body lava sub- sequently recovered as stated. MARRIAGE AT Runconx.—On Monday last, August 22, at the Runcorn Parish Church, by the Rev. Mr. Hughes, vicar of Cheswardyne, and late of Runcorn, Mr. John Alexander Cioedwell to Miss Emily Pearce. The wedding party and I, nests afterwards returned to Crofton Lodge to breakfast. The presents, which were numerous and costly, included a case of elver knives, forks, and spoons, silver salts, silver and other teapots, black marble timepiece, two china tea services, toilet sets, silver cruets, biscuit box, bread knife and board, fancy and table cloths, ttc. RUNCORN IMPROVEMENT COMMISSIONEES.—The annual

election 07 five gentlemen to represent the ratepayers of Runcorn on the Beard of Commissioners takes place on Thursday next, The retiring members are Messrs. W. Whittaker, F. A. Lake, Samuel Teylor, William Fisher, and William Handley. With the exception of Mr Handley, the gentlemen named intend to offer them- selves for re-election. Rumour has it that Mr. Joseph Williams, an old and respected servant of the public, will offer his services. It is also stated that Mr. P. Smith and ' Mr. S. Yarwood intend to seek the eutfrages of the rate- payers. UNDESIRAELE TENANTS AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn ' Police Court, on Monday, Thomas Blakemore, Thomas Sweeney, and Elizabeth Ellen Bird were charged with sleeping in an unoccupied house, and, havine no visible means of subsistence, failing to give a good account of themselves. At three o'clock on latinday morning Sergeant Woolley and Constable Sutton visited an empty house in Cooper-street. The doors were fastened, but Sutton got through the cellar window, and proceeding upetairs, found the prisoners sleeping there. They could give no account of themselvee, and stated they had no money, but at the police station Blakemore had 4d in his possession and Sweeney 2a lid. The woman had nothing. The prisoners were discharged with a caution. ASSAULT ote TEE POLICE AT WIDNES.—PaIt Haring- ton, a labourer, of St. Helens, was brought up at the Widnes Police Court on Monday charged with being drunk and disorderly, and also with assaulting P.C. Bowerbank. and damaging his whistle to the extent of Is Bd. On Saturday night the prisoner was very drunk, and wanted to light a man in Davies-street, Moss Bank. He refused to go away when regiested by P.C. Bewerhank, and that officer pro. ceeded to take him into custody. The prisoner, however, mule violent resistance, struck the constable between the eyes, and savagely kicked him. Several persons were re- quired to take the prisoner to the police station. The magistrates ordered the prisoner to pay 16s 8d and costs, or go to gaol for 21 days in default. He went to gaol. A Datieness TRAVELLER AT WIDNES.—,it Widnes Petty. Sessions, on Thursday, James Walker, a cotton porter from Liverpool, was charged with travelling from Edge Hill to Widnes without having previously paid his fare.—The pri• soner alighted from the train arriving in Widnes from Liverpool at 11.6 on Wednesday night. Dobson, the fore- man porter, asked him for his ticket, ano he replied that he had paid 7d to take him as far as he could, as be was out of work. Mr. Ashton, the chief booking clerk. gave the pri- soner into the custody of P.C. Coup, who, on searching bite, found a ticket from Lime street to Edge Hill and 5d upon him. Ile appeared very sleepy, as though he had re- cently awakened from a drunken sleep—The prisoner said he had been drinking, and did nut know how he got to Whines—The Bench imposed a fine of 24 63 and costs. ALLEGED DASTARDLY ASSAULT AT WIDNES.—At Wid- nes Police Court on Monday, Michael Cary, of Darold- street, and John Riley, of Elizabeth-street, rough looking young fellows, were charged with wounding a youog min named Matthew Butler, a cooper, of Ash-road. From a statement by Inspector Heigbley, it appeared that about midnight on Saturday Butler was standing at the Victoria. road entrance to the works of Messrs. Chattel], Deakin. and Cs, when trie prisoners and another young fellow came up. Riley, without the slightest provocation, struck Butler en the face with his clenched hand, and Butler ran into the works out of the way. The prisoners pursued him, knocked him down, and kicked him. Carr inflicted a severe wound on his forehead by kicking him there. As Dr. McCaw- bridge, who dressed t'•e wounds, was not present, the pri- soner was remanded for a week. AN APPLETON FARMER'S DIFFICULTIES.—ThOMAS Smith farmer, Appleton, on Thursday summoned to Widnes Police Court a boy named John Middlehurst for stealing turnips on the 18th August. A man named James Harper was charged with assaulting Smith at the same time and place It appeared from the evidence that Smith had lost nearly. half en acre of turnips throne' the depredations of loops and other persons. On the evening in question several lova were seen in the act of pulling up the turnips, and Middle- hurst was caught with a number in his possession. When Smith was walking him away along the field Harper came up and said "Let's have a fair understanding about this." Smith replied "What have you get to do with it ; get off the field." The defendant then struck Smith with his fist, and also butted him on the cheat with his head. He had previously had to ej•ct a man from the. field.—After hear- ing numerous witnesses the Bench fined Middlehurst Is and Costs 104 (id, and Harper 53 and costs lOs sd. TRE POKER AS A WEAPON AT WIDNES. At Widnes .Police Court,on Monday, before Mr. John Brock and Mr. EL W. Deacon, Margaret Dyes. wife of Thomas Dyes, a labourer, who lives at 94, Walmeley-street, was charged with unlawfully wounding Mary Daley, wife of John Daley, labourer, of SO. Wel meley-street. Inspector Kidehley ted that about a quarter to twelve on Saturday night there was a row proceeding in the street where the parties impli- cated live, and Mrs Daley went out of the house to see whit was the matter. The prisoner, who was quarrelling with a woman named H trrisoo, Field to Mrs Daley "You are going to stick up for the English, are you," at the same time seiz- ing hold of her hair and pulling her to the ground. The prisoner then ran into the house, and quickly returned with a poker, with which sbe struck Mrs Daley a severe blow on the head.—Mrs Daley gave evidence to this effect, and it was corroborated by a young girl—The prisoner denied using the poker, and alleged that Mrs Daley was the aggres- sor. The prisoner was remanded until Monday. She was I admitted to bail. . .
..... DREADFUL DEATH OF A WIDNES BIITCHEB.—A shocking -- •

fatality O-Ceu—rrer at Widnes, on Thursday. Wm. HoskeW, butcher, Widnes-road, assisted by a man named John Ball, on the morning of that day fetched a heifer from the farm of Mr. Glover, at Crouton. On the way the animal acted in a rather wild fashion, an I on arriving in Travis-street the men were unable to delve it into the slaughter-house of Mr. J. E. Johnson. The assistance of Mr. James Pemberton, mineral watet manufacturer, his two eons, and a servant named William Edwardson was obtained, bat with no better result, and at last Rocker placed a rope around the animal's neck. The lo,)se end of the rope became entangled round Hosker's leg and the cow, making a dash to run through the cordon of men around it, whirled Hoeker round several times, and lifted him off his feet. He fell heavily to the ground, and the back of his head corning into con- tact with the pavement was terribly smashed. After being dragged several yards by the infuriated beast Ito was picked I up by the by-standers, and Dr. McCambridge was quickly in attendance. Deczased died two hours later. Yesterday afternoon Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy coroner, held an Inquest on the body, aud a verdict of "Accidental death " was recorded. Hosker, who was only 37 years of age, leaves a widow and several children.

THE WIRRAL AND BIRKENHEAD AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY.—AII entries for this show close on Satur- day next. Intending exhibitors are requested to make their entries as early as convenient. VISIT OF THE ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY TO CHESHIRE.—Dr. Benson, Archbishop of Canterbury, will shortly pay a visit to Lord Egerton of Tatton, and during his stay will preach at Knutsford Church on behalf of the fund of the Chester Diocesan Girls' Friendly Society, of which Lord Egerton is president. CHILD BURNT 10 DEA= AT IRLAII.—An in-

quest was held on Wednesday evening at the Ship Hotel, Irlam, before Mr. F. Price, county coroner, touching the death of a child named Joseph Henry Kirkham, son of William Kirkham, farmer, Wood- stock Farm, Lower Irlam. On Friday night the deceased, who was three years and ten months old, whilst his mother was in another part of the house, upset a paraffin oil lainp which was burning on the table in the kitchen. His screams caused Mrs. Kirkham to run into the room, and she found the little fellow enveloped in flames. Before the fire could be extinguished the man s"ervant had to put him into a tub of water. He was severely injured all over the body, and although medical assist- ance was at once procured, he grew worse and died Non Monday night. The jury returned a verdict of accidental death.

THEATER ROYAL, RUNCORN.—A. special session Was held at Runcorn Police Court, on Monday, for the purpose of hearing an application for a license to perform stage plays at the Theatre Royal. Mr. W. R. Waldron made the appli- cation. In reply to Mr. Brundrit, Superintendent Hulling- worth, said he had examined the building and found it satis- factory. He had no objection to make —The Bench there- upon granted the license. FIRE AT Pax HILL, NEAR WIDNES.—Ott Tuesday after. neon a fire broke out on the estate of the Widnes Local Beard at Pex Hill. A large quantity of gorse and tbe wooden fencing round the reservoirs were all tibiae., but the Fire Brigade, under the superintendence of Mr. Lee' the assistant got manager, quickly quenched the flames. The loss is not very heavy. Fire again broke out amongst the gorse on Wednesday evening, but the services of the Fite Brigade were not required. WOUNDING AT WIDNES —Bridget Glynn was brought up at Widnes Petty Bessiens, on Thursday, charged with hav- ing, on the 20th August, unlawfully 'wounded Thomas Flaolgan by striking him on the head with a tumbler. F anigsn was still unable to appear, and the prismer was remanded until Monday. In the case of Ann Goulding, who is in gaol one charge of having, on the 13th instant, unlawfully wounded Elizabeth Tobin with a poker, a certi- ficate was produced showing that the prisoner was unfit to leave be gaol. The case was therefore defer ad until Monday. VISITORS TO BIACIPOOL Should stay at the Station Tem- perance Hotel, right opposite Central station. Central position. Commodious and accommodating. Terms easy. —Apply J. Heap.—Advt. THE NATIONAL DMUS &ND THE NORTEIWICH ELECTION. —At a late meeting of members of the T. P. O'Connor Branch of the Irish National League in Widnetetwo resolu- tions were unanimously carried, the first protesting against the action of the Government in proclaiming the National League,aed the second expressing the thanks of the League "to the electors of the Northwich Division for the manly way in which they have spoken in favour of giving the Irish people the rights of civil liberty," and also thanking " Mr Brunner for the straightforward manner in which he advo- cated the cause of justice and humanity during the recent election campaign. RUNNORN PRIMROSE LEAGUE AND LORD Hewitt Gnosvmeon.—A general meeting of the Runcorn Habita- tion of the Primrose League was held in Holy Trinity School. on Tuesday evening, Lady Brooke, ruling council- lor, presiding. WORKMEN'S EXCURSION FROM WIDNES —Messrs One- sage and Son, the celebrated manufacturers of seap, Wid• non, on Saturday last, gave the workmen in their employ their annual treat. In conformity with their usual custom Messrs Gossage chartered two railway trains, gave each man two tickets and le 61, and each apprentice who earned un- der 15s per week one ticket and a shilling. In addition to this display of generosity the men are permitted to choose where they will spend their holiday, and en the present oc- casion the majority were in favour of Llandudno, and be- fore seven o'clock on Saturday morning two laeg trains laden with a human freight of 1.200 souls, were speeding on their way to that "Queer of Welsh watering places." Under the charge of Inspector Carter, and Mr. McConnell, the station master, the journey was accomplished in excep- tionally good time, and without the slightest cause for alarm, the second excursion arriving at its destination by a quarter to ten. For the rest of the day " sweet will " was the only guide to pleasure, and whilst hundreds found their I enjoyment amongst the beauties of the immediate neigh- bourhood, and in smiling in the bay, others visited be coach and by boat the many charming spots further inland. The weather was of the most favourable description, and the whole of the excursionists enjoyed a most happy day. The chief office officials and the foreman accompanied the trip, and made every arrangement for the convenience and Com- fort of the travellers, who arrived safely home by half-past nine, It is not too much to say that this animal re-union of. tire men and their wives and sweethearts for a day's recrea- tion engenders s feeling of kindness and consideration be- tween masters and workmen that is to the benefit of both, and it, is to be regretted that the example set by Messrs Gossage is not more widely followed. There is news of Sir A. B Walker having rented a mansion and deer forest in Scotland for three months; but one does not hear anything of the marriage that was announced. Can it be that he has turned aside from the dear to the deer?

It is stated that the Hessian fly has ap- peared on a farm at High Leigh, and that samples of the eggs and of corn will be sent to the Agricultural Department of the Privy Council. That Hessian fly is a nuisance. Why does it not stop at home ? Wonder if the fly would flee if attacked with Hessian boots?

James Billington, who executed Hobson at Armley Gaol, was formerly a collier, but has for some time followed the occupation of a barber, having a shop in Market-street, Farnworth, near Bolton. He is 39 years of age, is sit. din. in height, dark, but a rather pleasant face. He is a local preacher—and why not? After a little further experience, he will be well able, in a sermon, to point a moral and adorn a tale.

A number of St. Helens Volunteers took part in the annual county shooting contests at Altcar on Friday and Saturday, and their success is most extraordinary. Their money winnings amoutted to £145, and the cups they carried off are valued at £3OO. It will be remembered that the St. Helens men came out well in the shooting at Wim- bledon. And now they have carried off several cups but let them not use the cups, or the hand may lose its cunning.

--- It would seem that the present season will see the end of bands in Bank Park. The' music is charming, the people attend in thousands, but they are so absorbed that they quite overlook the collection. The total amount collected for the season is 4z los 9d. Orpheus might have been able to move stones, but he would have had a hard task if he had tried to reach the pockets of Warrington admirers. They really cannot think, when there is music in the air, of filthy lucre.

The Conservative party in Warrington su3- tain a great loss by the resignation of Cap- tain Reynolds as chairman. They have tried hard to induce him to reconsider his de- cision, but to no purpose. And he is quite right. Health, as Emerson says, is the first wealth. The "wear and tear" of two Par- liamentary contests in two years is something terrible to a chairman who does his duty to his party. And there is no denying that Captain Reynolds has done his duty.

It was scarcely gracious of Councillor Jolley, in suggesting Mr. Robert Pierpoint as a successor, to say "he was the most popular man they had in Warrington." It was quite enough to make both Captain Reynolds and Sir Gilbert think it' was time to take a back seat. But it is always the way—" The King is dead; long live the King !" By-the-bye, how is it that the Con- servatives came to talk about an illuminated address to the Captain? Can they not raise the money for that other testimonial to him for which subscriptions were sought over twelve months ago? The great demonstration in Dublin, on Tuesday, to protest against the proclamation of the National League, was made note- worthy by English M.P.'s taking part in it. Irishmen have, with some reason, complained that Englishmen have not sufficiently frater- nised with them; but there is to be an end of difficulties of that kind. We are getting a step nearer the time when, as Burns has it, "men to men the world o'er shall brothers be for a' that."

The resignation of Mr. T. W. Russell. M.P., following in the heels of that of Colonel Maude, the hon. secretary to the Liberal Unionists, has not a little disturbed Lord Hartington. Mr. Russell is a vigorous speaker, he is thoroughly in earnest, and we may be sure he means what he says when he proclaims that the mutilated Irish Land Bill will bring mischief to Ireland. He still avers that he is a Liberal Unionist, although he refuses to act with them. Odd, isn't it?

The system of hirinz furniture seems to be pretty prevalent at Runcorn, and, judging from the numerous appeals to the County Court, it is anything but a good one. There were two cases before the court on Tuesday but when the agreements were put in it was found that they were drawn up as if full pay- ment had been made when the goods were obtained. There had been payments of instalments, but the judge said he could not go behind the written agreements, and gave a verdict for the defendants. It is a matter of course to say that the plaintiffs were " nonsuited."

It is sad to think that two lives have been lost at Widnes. in twelve months, in playing football. Commenting on the fact at the in- quest, on Monday, on the young man Bellis, who was killed on Tuesday week, the deputy- coroner remarked that these deaths snowed that "either the players were very rough or this game was a rough one." The game is undoubtedly a rough one; but there is no suspicion in this case of any foul play. The game was played in a friendly manner; and it was a matter of course to bring in a verdict of "Accidental Death," but it is a death nevertheless.

The automatic sweetmeat machines ought to be abolished. They place temptation un- necessarily in the way of boys, and some of them become criminals before they know properly what they are about. Four lads were summoned at Liverpool, on Monday. for obtaining chocolate from the machines by putting in pieces of lead or cardboard instead of a penny. It is satisfactory to see that the magistrates discharged the lads on their promising not to offend again. It is a pity the owners of the machines cannot be sum- moned for leading lads into temptation.

- SHIP CANAL PREPAHATIONS.—It is stated that the Manchester Ship Canal Company will shortly commence the erection of a wooden building, at Latchford, to accommodate about 200'men who will be engaged in the construction of the canal. People living in houses along the line ,of the proposed canal have received notice of the intention of the Company to proceed with the works. Amongst those who hat% received notice is his Wershie the Mayor, Alderman Pickmere. It may be added that in Latchford about 100 houses are in course of erection, building in this part of Cheshire having been stimulated by the Ship Canal project. " PUNCH " ON TILE RECEPTION OF Mn. BRUNNER. —The following is from Toy's "Essence of Par- liament" in this week's " ninch ":—" Tuesday. John Manners in his place to-night. Everyone glad to see him back again; Liberals, Conservatives, Dissentients. Unionists, whatever we be, all unite in saying a friendly word to John on his convales- ence. Another arrival greeted with more mixed feelings. Brunner, flushed by his great victory in Northwich, comes up to be sworn in. Tremendousl cheering on Liberal side. Dead silence among Ministerialists. Old Morality gazes up at glass roof with preoccupied air ; thoughts far away from Westminster or Northwich either. Caine, looking on from Bar, turns his back, and marches forth. 'Another blessing in disguise,' says he. 'I think now I'll go off to Japan, and see how they're getting on with their projected Parliamentary Institu- tions. Might get somo hints for forming our National l'arty." ROYAL MANCHESTER Snow.—A meeting of the Council and members of the Royal Manchester, Liverpool, and North Lancashire Agricultural Society was held on the show ground at Old Traf- ford on Wednesday, when the names of the success- ful competitors in seeds and farming were announ- ced. The Secretary (Mr. Rigby) stated that invita- tions had been received from Barrow and Blackpool to hold the next year's show in those towns. The meeting, after considering the merits of the respec- tive places, decided to adjourn the seleation of the town until Thursday next. Mr. Rigby informed the meeting that the preparations for holding this year's show at Old Trafford were in an advanced state, and would no doubt be completed in time for the opening on Wednesday next. Among the awards were the following ;—Best arable farm, above 80 acres and under 150 acres, first prize £l5, Mr. J. R. Newton. Warburton, Lymm; best farm of mixed husbandry, about half stock and half arable, above 150 acres, first prize £2O, Messrs: J. and J. Percival, Parkside, Aston, Preston Brook ; prize for the woman servant long- est with the same master, Elizabeth Goulds, 16 years with Mr. Peter Davies, of Warburton. FATAL FOOTBALL ACCIDENT AT WIDNES. Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy coroner, on Monday held an icqaest at the Simms Cress Hotel, Widnes. on the body of Thomas Bellls, aged 21, a moulder, who died on Timis- day night, in consequeace of injuries received whilst play- ing football at Farnworth on Tuesday evening. . . . .

The father of the deceaeed stated that his son did not Play football regularly, because be was opposed to his son's engaging in the game. Deceased was quite well when he returned home from work at eix o'clock on Tuesday even- ing. He went out again and was brought home at half- past ten uncenecious, and was at once pat to bed. lie told witness that he had been hurt whilst playing football, hay- ing been struck by one of the players named Evans. De- ceased did net wish to blame anybody for what had been done, as he believed the injury was caused accidentally. He was attended by Dr. M‘Ciimbridge, but died from the in- juries received on the following Thureday night. Elijah Broome, a fireman at the works of Messrs. Butch. Mem and Sone, said on Tuesday evening he was playing football at Ferovrortli. It wee simply a game amongst the members of the club for practice. The players, with the exception of the deceased, were all member of the Fern. worth Football Club. A the time the accident occurred, witness was running with the ball and livane c tiled him to pass. Witness was then surrounded by bie opponents, and he threw the ball, as he thought, to Evans. but that player did not receive it. Bellis, however, secured it, but how he disposed of it witness could not say. Deceased had only b,eu playing the game about five minutes when the acci- dent occurred. The game was conducted in as fair a way as possible. A boy told him that Bellis was hurt, and wit- ness at once stopped the game, and with Evans ran to the assistance of the deceased. They asked him what had hap- p.ined, and he at first said that witness had kicked him, but afterwards be admitted that he did not know how he had been injured. They at first carried the deceased to a public- house, and gave him some brandy and soda, and then took him to the surgery of Dr. O'Neil, but as the doctor was not in they took him home, deceased insleting upon walking all the way. _ . .

Dr. M'Ca.nbridge said he was called to see the deceased on the night of Turnday last, and found kim very weak and suffering great pain over the abdomen, but particularly on the right groin. Witness made a post-mortem examination, and found that there bad been strangulation of the bowels. There were no external marks of violence except general blackness. If deceased had been "butted" or kicked during the game, he considered that this would be likely to cause the injuries which canted the death of the deceased. Fleury °randy, one of the players, said there was no qitar- rel between Evans and the deceased, but the former told him that Balls came against his leg while the game was pro- ceeding. John Evans, who desired to give evidence, said the de- ceased, In passing the ball, stumbled against his knee. Wit- Mee had never quarrelled with Bellis, and had always been on good terms with bim. Mr. Husband, in addressing the jury, said it was much to be regretted that that was the second death in Widnes in twelve months arising out of the game of football, and it showed that either the players were very rough or the game was a rough one. Inasmuch as certain statements had been made in regard to how the accident occurred, he considered it his duty to have the presence of the doctor, in case of a verdict which would entail further proceedings. He wae, however, glad to find that the game was carried out In a very friendly manner by all the players. Everyone knew that football games were not al ways fairly played, bat he thought that in this instance the persons who took part in the game were exonerated (rent blame, and that the injuries were caused purely by an accident. The jury agreed with the remarks of the deputy•coroner, and returned a verdict of" Accidental death."

STACK OF COIL 011 FlRE.—Presornably as a result of the heat and drought, an enormous stack of coal, containing 15,000 tons, On the property of Messrs. A. Knowles and Sons at Little Lever, has been on fire for several days past. Much loss was caused, not only by Consumption, but in re- moving some thousands of tons of coal in order to reach the seat of the fire. ALLEGED CHILD MIIRDEE.—A t telfast, on Wednesday, a lab mrer named John Spence, and his wife were, committed for trial, charged with the murder of their infant child, who, it is alleged, after being beaten in a barbarous manner by the male prisoner, was dashed by him into a vessel of boiling water. The child, which was entered in a burial society, died a few hours afterwards in terrible agony. The case was reported to the police by a neighbour who heard the child's screams. THE BOLTON BTRIKE: HELP PROM IRELAND.—At the strike Committee meeting, on Tuesday morning, it was atatrd that the deputation seat to Ireland on Saturday, to lay the claims of the men before the people there, bad met with a most clattering reception at Dublin, and a large re- mittance is expected from there this week. The Dublin Trades Council, and the Irish Labour League, passed reso- lutions, after hearing the members of the deputation, to the effect that the action of the Bolton engineers was justifiable, and their cause recommended to the support of all honour- able men. The joint committee of the men met on Monday evening, ktit came to no decision upon the Mayor's amended proposals for arbitration.

The match between Warrington and Broughton, on Sat- urday, when nearing its conclusion, unfortunately had to be abandoned owing to a dispute. Lttle interest remained in the match between Lancashire and Notts, at Manchester, on Saturday, as Notts, with seven wickets down for 83, still required 25 runs to avert an innings defeat. Flay began at noon. The innings closed for 114, Lancashire requiring six runs to win. Briggs's seven wickets cost 53 runs. Mr. Hornhy sent in Stagg and Barlow, Attewell and Barnes bowling. Barlow bit a two, and Sugg a four, and Lancashire won by ten wickets. A brilliant batting achievement by Mr. E. Sainsbury marked the opening of the annual cricket week at Taunton on Monday, when, in fine weather, the retnrn match be- tween Somerset and Hants was commenced. Going in first for the home side, on a run-getting wicket, Mr. Sainsbury was batting for four hours without giving a chance, compil- ing 164 runs out of a total of 315. His chief hits were twenty fours, seven threes, and twelve twos. The game between Lancashire and Sussex, which has caused so great an interest, ended on Wednesday in a vic- tory for Lancashire by four wickets. When stumps were drawn overnight, Sussex had completed both innings, and Lancashire their first, with a result that left the last-named county 204 to obtain ere they could claim a victory. Though so much was before them the Lancashire team set to the task with a will, and most people capable of judging were not sanguine of Sussex securing the victory when it was seen how well the wicket played on hostilities being re- sumed. That Mr. Hornbv did not mean to throw a chance away soon became evident, as he started batting much more carefully than is his wont, and to his and Sugg's exertions the victory by so mane as four wickets is due. Sugg, curiously enough, scored exactly the same total as in his first innings, and played very fine cricket, his defence being excellent, whilst his hitting, when opportunity offered, was well timed and brilliant. The 812439 X men did all they could to avoid defeat, their bowling and fielding being alike creditable, and, after the good fight they made against a team that so recently proved in great form by causing both Surrey and Notts to strike their colours, they should look with confidence to the future. Score—Sussex, 147 and 252; Lancashire, 196 and 204, with four wickets to spare. Oa Wednesday, the contests between Yorkshire and Notts, ana Surrey and Kent, were drawn. Middlesex were victorious ever Gloucestershire by one wicket, and Somer.. setshire beat Hants by six wickets.
OUR LONDON, LETTER.
LONDON. THURSDAY.

The circumstances under which the Government have proclaimed the National League are strikingly illustrative of their hapless position. Goaded on by the yelping of the "Times," which accurately represents the views of the landlords and the Orangemen, restrained by the opposition of their allies the Dissentient Liberals, and confronted by public opinion, as expressed at Northwich and elsewhere, they put off decision till the last mo- ment. Then, as often happens with weak people, they suddenly decided to do something, and valorously announced the proclamation of the League. But hereinthey hedged themselves about with an ingenious device. The League is pro- claimed, and thereby the noisy set among their supporters are gratified. But no real harm is done, as, before the executive come into conflict with the League, it will be necessary for an order to be issued prohibiting meetings of the League in par- ticular places. Thus, though they seem to have done a great deal and have, indeed, excited public opinion throughout the country they are not really ' committed to any irrevocable act. How far their relations with the Dissentient Liberals have been affected by the proclamation may probably be known contemporaneously with the publication of this letter. It is no secret (Mr. Chamberlain has 'indeed publicly announced the fact) that Lord Hartington and himself were opposed to the pro- clamation, and had advised the Government against it. Mr. Chamberlain has gone farther, and declares his intention to vote against the Government on 1, the issue raised by Mr. Gladstone. Lord Hartington, as is his habit, has been more reticent with respect to his intentions, and the most that can be expected of him is that he should abstain from voting. However this be, the Govern- inent will, of course, have a majority, though its Comparative smallness may serve as a useful warn- ing. Their more prosperous days are evidently over,. Some of the Dissentient Liberals, headed by Mr. Chamberlain, have broken the spell by voting against them, which, once done, may be repeated with dangerous ease. Conservatives are confidently Counting upon Lord Hartington joining the Gov- ernment. But that grows less and less an import- ant event. They have discovered in the case of Mr. Goschen, a much abler man than Lord Harting- ton, that, when a man puts off his old opinions and goes over, haft and baggage, into the enemy's camp, he loses all his personal weight and importance. When in the Parliament of 1880 Mr. Goschen was accustomed to pose between the two comba- tants, there were few men in the House of Commons who exceeded him in personal power. Now his interposition in debate does not carry more weight than does that of Lord George Hamilton or Baron de Worms. The accession of Lord Hartington to the Tory ranks would not mean the permanent addition of a dozen votes. If he went over before the beginning of next session, as it is reported he will do, he would take with him twenty, or perhaps thirty, of the Whigs who al-' ready habitually vote with the Government. But/ this Parliament will not last for ever. There must come the day of Dissolution, and then where will these gentlemen be? The House of Commons is becoming a dreadfully desolate place. To-night, of course, in anticipation of the great speech from Mr. Gladstone, and in response to urgent whips, the benches were fairly filled. But on earlier nights there have been chiefly

empty benches for orators to address The only approach to excitement on an ordinary night is the news that some fortunate member has secured a pair. Other members less happy eagerly discuss the stroke of good luck, and wish it may presently come to them. There is nothing like obstruction of the kind that handicapped Mr. Gladstone's Go- vernment from 1881 onwards. The Irish members, in truth, are very little in the House, being more usefully engaged in electioneering campaigns. But there is sore lack of a master hand. Matters drift in most melancholy fashion, and though the House meets early and sits late very little progress is made. An example of the incompetence of the manage- ment is found in connection with Saturday sittings. When, in times when obstruction was a reality, it was found necessary to sit on Saturdays,it was taken in the usual manner and no limit put to the sitting. I remember very well in the first hour of a Sunday morning the Puritanism of Mr. Philip Cal- lan was shocked that the House of Commons should still be sitting. Having' to take. Saturdays, Mr. Smith, in his feeble iashion of trying to walk on _
both sides of the road at the _same time, announced

, that the Rules which prevailed on Wednesdays would be applicable to the Saturday—that is to say, the House meeting at noon would rise at six. The con- sequence was shown last Saturday, the House being compelled to cut short its deliberations on the'stroke of six, when just on the verge of deciding a ques- tion that had occupied the whole of the sitting. For all practical purposes meyibers might as well have been making holiday. Mr. O'Donnell, who has been living at Aix-la- Chapelle, has come over to London to prepare his case against the "Times." It can hardly come on before December, and I understand that efforts will , be made to postpone it till February, in order to meet the convenience of many members of Parliament who will be subpcenad. Amongst these are Mr. Par- nell, Mr. Justin McCarthy, ex-President of the Land League in Great Britain, Mr. John Dillon, Mr. Arthur O'Connor, and Mr. T. P. O'Connor, who as president of the League in Great Britain, will be required to produce all its books and minutes. Mr. Gladstone will also be called, with some of his col- leagues who can throw light on the circumstances under which Lord Frederick Cavendish was appoin- ted to the Irish Secretaryship, and can explain the results of the Government examination into the circumstances of his assassination. Mr. O'Donnell ,is determined that a clean breast shall be made of everything conhected with the Irish Land League,. more especially in connection with the distribution of the dollars, an anxiety which, curiously enough, striatly coincides with that expressed by the defen- dant in the case. Mr. O'Donnell tells me that Mr. Arthur O'Connor and some other of the Irish party sympathise with him in his conflict with the " Times," whilst others look upon what certainly will be a searching examination with apprehension. It seems a big undertaking with inadequate forces, for the attack. But those who know Mr. O'Donnell and have been witness of exhibitions of his tenacity of purpose, know that when he means buineas he will carry it out. A movement amongst the English Ambassadors abroad is on the cards. Lord Lyons, it is said, is at last going to leave Paris, whither Sir Edward Malet will migrate, and Sir Henry Wolff will go to Berlin. This seems incredible after the lamentable failure of his mission to the East. But nothing is impossible to a Conservative Government when a job is to be accomplished. The prolonged sitting of Parliament keeps a good i many people n London. But a stroll through the West End shows that that part of the great metropo- lis is really "empty." Drawn blinds and brown I paper pasted over the windows testify to the flight from many mansions. The Park is deserted, Bond- street is passable, and the incessant roll of carriages seen but the other day in Regent-street has passed away. We have had this season a tremendous colony of Americans. But they, too, are flitting. One of Messrs. Cook's agents told me thaL the season which-they regard as nearly over was th 6 busiest remembered, but that the demand for tickets, Oiefly for the Continent, was swelled by the AmeriN..ns. On the other hand, America is becoming more and more the happy holiday ground of Englishmen. I Very nearly a quorum of the House of Commons, and much More than a quorum of th 3 House of Lords, are already in the United States, or are pre- paring for the voyage ;thither.

div.head: TIN LATE MR. ALDERMAN PEARSON'S
div.p: TIN LATE MR. ALDERMAN PEARSON'S
WILL.

The will, with one codicil, of the late Mr. John Pearson, J.P., of Golborne Park, Newton-le-Willows, who died on the 2nd of June last, was proved on the 17th inst., by the four executors and trustees, Mr. Jacob Higson, of Manchester, engineer; Mr. Frank John Leslie, of Liverpool, solicitor; and two of testator's sons, Mr. Thomas Henry Pearson, of Golborne Park, and Mr. George Frederick Pearson, of Pwllheli, North Wales. The personal estate was sworn at £188,866. The will is dated the 18th October, 1886, and the codicil the 24th May, 1887. The testator bequeaths to his widow absolutely such carriages, horses, plate, and furniture as she may select. After various small bequests to rela- tives and 100 guineas to each of the executers named in his will, he bequeaths £4,000 towards the erection and endowment of a new church now being built at Lower Ince, being the balance unpaid at the date of his will of the sum promised by him, in conjunction with his partner, the late Mr. Knowles, M.P., for that purpose. His property in New Zea- land he gives to his two sons resident there to be divided between them. Special provision is made for the carrying on of the business inwhich be was interested at his death, including his Welsh slate quarries. All the residue of his estate real and perscnal is devised and bequeathedtohissaid trusteesintrust to invest £20,000 for the benefit of his widow, and £14,000 for each of his daughters. The residue of his estate and effects is to be divided equally among his sons, it being directed that the various properties given to them by the testator in his life- time are to be treated as gifts, and are not to be taken into account in any way in connection with the division under the will.
MYSTERIOUS DEATH OF A CHILD.

At the Patten Arms Hotel, Warrington, on Tues- day morning, Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy coroner, held an inquest on view of the body of a child named Emily Jones, whose death took place at the Infirmary on Sunday, under rather remarkable /cir- cumstances, which were narrated in the evidence adduced by the witnesses.—The first witness called was Emily Jones, wife of Thomas Jones, of 17, Philip-street, a labourer, who said that the body of the deceased was that of her daughter,Emily Jones, who was nine years of age. Last Saturday week deceased went out into the fields with the baby for a walk. She returned at about noon, and com- plained elan ache in her leg. On Sunday she.] told witness that on Saturday she had fallen ' over a stone and hurt her leg. Witnesa bathed the part which she complained of with salt and water, and on Monday she bathed it with vinegar and saltpetre. Witness called in the In- firmary doctor on Tuesday. Dr. J. T. Smith atten- ded to deceased, who was ultimately taken to the Infirmary. Witness next saw her daughter on the Friday, when she was no better. On Saturday morning she was a little better, but on Sunday morning witness got a message that deceased was worse. She went to the Infirmary and was told that inflammation of the•lungs had set in. Deceased died-on Sunday night.—Dr. John T. Smith, assistant house surgeon at the Infirmary, said he saw the deceased on the 16th instant for the first time, at her mother's house. She was suffering from a frac- ture of the leg, the outer bone only, and was also feverish. Witness sent a lotion to put on the leg. He next saw her again on Thursday. She was less feverish then. He did not admit her to the Infirmary on the first occasion because he was afraid she might take some infectious disease into the hospital. She was at- tended to at the Infirmary, but got rapidly worse, and died on Sunday. In the opinion of the witness neither the fracture nor the inflammation of the lungs was sufficient to cause death. An ordinary broken bone would not account for thefeverishness. The deceased certainly had some other disease, the nature of which could not be arrived at without a post mortem examination, which had not been ordered. Drs. White, Starkey Smith, and Joseph saw the child, and they were all unable to arrive at a satisfactory diagnosis of the intense feverishness. —The Coroner said that the jury could return an open verdict to the effect that the deceased died at the hospital, having been admitted with a fractured leg, and also having suffered from inflammation of the lungs. or they could order that a post mortem ex- amination should be made.—The ury considered that as there were no suspicious circumstances in the case, an examination was not necessary, and returned an open verdict.

The following is a list of the applications to be made at the adjourned licensing sessions next week :—For new victuallers' provisional licenses: (1) Greenall, Whitley, and Company, Brewers, Limited, new house to be built in lloyle-street ; (2) Greenall, Whitley, and Company, Brewers, Limited, new house to be built in Battersby-lane. For, full alehouse licenses: (1) Blijah Lawton. Bewsey-road, "The Grove," now holding an off-license for beer, wines, and spirits; (2) Henry Morte, Battersby-lane, now holding a similar off-license.

RENEWAL OF ALE HOUSE LICENSES. The Chief Constable handed in the defaulter sheet for the year with regard to the business of publicans. He had received no objections to the renewals of licenses. Mr. White (magistrate's clerk) : Henry Gittens, of the Swan Inn, Bridge- street, has been twice fined during the year—.£s each time—once for having his house open during prohibited hours, and once for suffering gaming on the premises. The license was not endorsed in either case. It is proposed to adjourn this case to the Adjourned Brewster Sessions, so that anyone wishing to make an objection against the renewal can do so.—Alderman' Davies said that on that statement the justices would adjourn- it. He thought that in a case of this kind a recommenda- tion should be entered in the minute book to the effect that if there is recurrence of offences during the coming tNN 7e months, the license should be forfeited at the licensing day next ensu- ing.—Councillor Greening: I think that is a proper course.—Alderman Davies: I mean on the licensing day twelve months hence; if it occurs within the next twelve months the license will be forfeited.— The whole of the licenses, with the exception of the one referred to, were then renewed.

div.head: RENEWAL OF BEERHOUSE LICENSES. – – –
div.p: RENEWAL OF BEERHOUSE LICENSES. - - -

Chief Constable Hunt said that there were no ob- jections to the renewals. The occupier of the Gun Imrhad been brought up for two offences on one day; he was convicted on one and dismissed -on the other. He was still the occupier of the Gun Inn, which had been fairly conducted since.—The Chairman observed that the offences took place nearly twelve mionths ago.—The beerhouse licenses were all renewed.
OFF-LICENSES. • No charge bad been brought against the holders of off-licenses during the year, and their licenses were now renewed.
BILLIAMDS IN THE SMALL HOURS.

Richard Bircball applied for the renewal of a bil- liard license for premises in Scotland-road, op- posite the Theatre Royal.—Chief Constable Hunt said that several magistrates had called his atten-, tion to the late hours at which the billiard room was open. The license allowed the holder to open until one o'clock, flirt time being regulated by Act of Parliament.—Alderman Davies asked if the magis- trates could fix the time at twelve o'clock.—The Magistrates' Clerk: No, sir; the act fixes the time. —Chief Constable Hunt said there was ho complaint against the holder of the license.—Alderman Davies observed that it was not desirable to encourage any- one to play billiards after .12 o'clock at night.—The renewal of the license was then granted. This was all the business.

div.head: RAILWAY SERVANT KILLED AT WARRING TON. A `WARNING TO PORTERS. ,
div.p: A RAILWAY SERVANT KILLED AT WARRING TON. A `WARNING TO PORTERS. ,

Shortly after noon, on Saturday' a porter in the employ of the London and North-Western Railway Company, at Bank Quay Station, Warrington, was endeavouring to cross the line when he was caught by a train from Chester that was entering the sta- tion, and killed on the spot. His mangled remains were at once removed to the Patten Arms Hotel to await an inquest, and the police were informed of what had occurred. The deceased, who was a very respectable man, was named Samuel Stephenson and had been Jiving in lodgings in Dixon-street. He was unmarried. Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy coroner, held an inquiry regarding the death at the Patten Arms Hotel on Tuesday morning, when evid- ence to the following effect was taken. Mr. Fenna, of Chester, appeared on behalf of the railway com- pany. William Stephenson, ather of the deceased, ,who Ilives at 28, Ismay-street,,Liverpool, said that he had identified the body now lying at the Patten Arms as that of his son, Samuel Stephenson. Deceased was 26 years of age, and had lodged at 33, Dixon- street, Warrington. He was a platform porter un- der the London and North-Western Railway Com- pany, at Bank Quay Station. His hearing and eye- sight were both good. , William Trevett, 48, Parker-street, Warrington, a porter at Bank Quay Station,said that on Saturday, at 12-15 in the afternoon, he was standing on the, , down aide of the high level at the Statism. He saw deceased standing in the four foot. Deceased was crossing the line when someone called to him and he turned round. The train from Chester, due at Warrington at 12-15 was coining in. Deceased saw it coming and seemed frightened, fot he turned round to go back to the platform. Witness saw him put his band on the buffer of the engine. The engine knocked him down and he was killed. It was a woman who shouted and stopped deceased.— The Coroner: How is it that you porters all seem to try how near you can shave it when you cross the line. , Have you no proper Instructions about crossing a line in front of a train.—Witness: Yes, sir.—The Coroner,: Stationmasters and porters alike seem to do it. My words do not apply to everyone, although all those I have noticed have been the same.—ln answer to a juryman, witness said that sometimes one set of porters worked both platforms. If the porters on one side saw two or three in atten- dance on the other they need not cross over. The stationmaster would fine them if he saw them croa- sing when there was no need,—A juryman: Pas- sengers are prohibited from crossing.—The Coroner: I Passengers do not always see the danger, and per- haps do not see a train coming, but the porters seem to wait until practically the last moment., and then to cross the line.—A juryman: Did you hear what the woman said when she called to deceased? —Witness: No.—Another juryman: She might see himin danger and call out to warn him.—ln answer to further questions, witness said that the deceased was dragged some distance by the train. Ralph Brett, of Chester, an engine driver in the employ of the company, said that on Saturday he was driver of the engine that was due to arrive at Warrington from Chester at 12-15. As he was en- tering the station, he saw the legs of the deceased. The left carriage was dragging deceased along. Wit- nes stopped the train as soon as he possibly could. He did not see anything of the deceased crossing the line before the engine struck him. He had been a driver for sixteen years.—The Coroner: What is,

The Stock Exchange still exhibits the hall-mark of stagnation. has been ite chief characteristic this Sold by all Grocers and Druggists,tn canisters, month. This.which after all is due to the absence ef speculative Id., 10d.. and le Id. each business, as there has continued to be a considerable amount eihni.saislir JI4.ICDIIIIII I EON. err of steady buying for country clients who rightly re- gard the present time as most favourable for investing. Home Rails have been especially depressed, due to a large extent to the unfavourable traffic returns of the past week, which in many of the leading liaes is very heavy. Great Western have decreased £3,980, Sheffield £1,492, and North British £3,847, while the continued decrease in Metropolitan traffic has caused a decline of fully two for the week in the price of stock. Per contra industrial companies have shown considerable buoyancy, Vie shares ef Hoskiss and E.G. Pow- der having risen nearly a half. . The American market is still irregular, prices on this side being nominally better than in New York. Hudson Bay shares, to which attention Was called in these columns recently, have steadily improved, and are fully three- quarters better than when attention WAS first called to them, and the future of this stock points to a still further rise. The announcement of the completion of the scheme for reorganising the Mexican National Railway Company is the most important news from the other side during the week. The line will be ready in about twelve months. Until Wednesday it was fully expected that a further rise would be made in the bank rate, as it was anticipated that fu.ther shipments of gold would be made for America, but this having been postponed, the directors made no alteration in the rate on Tharaday, which remains at 3 per cent., but it is fully anticipated that the hardening of the money market is only delayed. Company promoters are still on tour.and they are unani- mous in regarding the present as fatal to any company if brought out, but it is said that there are fully a hundred ready for the public when the time is regarded as satiefac-

tory. The shares in the Ridsdale Railway Lamp and Lighting Cornpauv have been actively inquired for on the strength of the company having already disposed of patent rights, and that a dividend of In per cent leas been paid.

WARRINGTON STA RR-BOWK ETT BOLDING SOCIETY. On Monday evening, a well attended meeting was held in Legh-street Primitive Methodist School- room, the occasion of the gathering being the taking of a ballot for the third appropriation of the War- rington (826) Starr-Bowkett Building Society. The chair was taken by Mr. John Walker, and amongst those also present were Messrs. Owen (Widnes), Griffiths, Gregg, Crompton, Burton, and Titchett (secretary). The CHAIRMAN said they were met to make the third appropriation of the Warrington Starr Bowkett Building Society. Be was glad to be able to state that the society was making satisfactory progress, as there were now 303 members with 662 shares. The chief interest that he had in taking part in societies of that kind was that they were great aids to thrift. Unfortunately the people of this country had not acquired habits of saving to the extent in which they had been acquired in some countries on the Continent. The peasantry of France were especially careful of their earnings, so much so that when the great war indemnity was demanded by Germany after the war,. it was found that the peasantry of France were in a position to find the bulk of the money. Some of the working-classes of this country seemed to think that with small earn- ings it was impossible to begin saving, but there appeared to be no difficulty in finding money to spend upon intoxicating liquor. He thought, so long as they were spending over 120 millions a year in intoxicating drinks that there was great room for taking a new course and laying something aside for a rainy day. After deciding to begin to save money, the difficulty with most people was to be sure that they had a safe investment, and in this respect he thought the Starr-Bowkett Building Societies offered them a special advantage. They might have what might be regarded as a safe in- vestment in Savings Banks, but, unfortunately, the interest was low, and they might take it that, as a general rule, where the interest was exceedingly high the security was doubtful. By means of Starr- Bowkett Building Societies people had what might be called absolute security, and at the same time they got in the long run good interest for t heir money. Mr. Walker then proceeded to give details of a compa- rison between the result of placing money in an investment society at 5 per cent., and the Starr Bowkett Building Society under ordinary condi- tions, and showed that the result was greatly in favour of the Starr Bowkett Building Society. It was a point to consider that the rules of their societies were framed so as to protect, at every point, the interests of the investor. The fines were small, and provision was made for people who were unable to pay through being ill or out of work. It was a noteworthy fact with regard to these societies that not in a single instance had a mortgage been foreclosed upon the property ac- quired by any working-man who was a member of these societies. He also said there was no specula- tion in the Starr-Bowkett Societies, as there was in some other societies, with the money invested. It be- came by appropriation the property of one of the members who made his own investment, and thus got the benefit, if there was a benefit, and sustained the loss himself if there was a loss. Some Permanent Benefit Build- ing Societies had found when times were good that they had more moneythan they could satisfactorily invest. They had consequently been led into spe- culation, and, in one instance which the chairman named, the society advanced large sums upon a colliery undertaking. The result was that some thousands of pounds were lost, and the bulk of the members had lost every penny they had in the so- ciety. In conclusion, he urged that self help, after all, was the best help, and, as the old adage had it, God helped those who helped themselves. They should save xot with the view of becoming stingy or miserly, but in the language of Burns. for "the glorious privilege of being independent:' (Ap- plause.) Mr. Owns; in the course of an address explanatory of the Starr-Bowkett system; remarked that time was when there was very little co-operation in this country, but the people were improving in habits of thrift, and were learning how to look out for a rainy day. Benefit societies were rapidly increas- ing and gaining in strength; there was co-operation by means of unity in trade, there was unity for the purpose of supplying food and furnishing houses, and there was unity for the purpose of providing houses in which to dwell. All this must materially tend to the advantage of the working classes. Vast sums of money were by this means collected, and judiciously invested in various undertakings for the benefit of the many. Referring more particularly to the Starr-Bowkett Societies, he explained the safe basis on which they are conducted, a basis which makes loss through any means almost an im- possibility, as the secretaries are guaranteed, and there is a system of banking the money received in subscriptions that entirely precludes the possibility of fraud, as by that.vstem the directors of a society are kept construithr informed of the money received and deposited. it was utterly impossible for a sec- retary to "do' the society out of more than one night's takings. On this point a member present instanced a case. in which a secretary had absconded. Mr. Owen said that there must have been neg- ligence on the part of the directors, and explained that as there was a guarantee, the society did not lose anything. (Applause.) After further conversation had taken place with regard to the system. Mr. Ikin gave a recitation, and the business of the ballot was then proceeded with. Mr. Alfred Dunn and Mr. 11. Bond were ap- pointed scrutineers, and Master Frederick Charles Stringer was selected to draw the ballot balls. On the numbers 209 being declared, the Secretary said that the holder of that number was one week be- hindhand with his subscriptions, and could not therefore have the benefit of the appropriation. The CHArnitAx I hope this will be a lesson to everhodY. (Hear, hear)—On another ballot being taken, number 298 was drawn, and Mr. John Budge, of Bewsey-road, Warrington, who is the holder of four shares, became entitled to £4OO free of interest for 14 years. The meeting concluded with a vote of thanks to the Chairman.

The Earl of Dumfries, son of the Marquis of Bate, on Wednesday opened a new dock at Cardiff, and subsequently the Marchioness of Bute cut the first sod of a public park which has been presented to the town by the Marquis. NEWTON 110IITICIILTUR4L SOCIETY.—As will be seen from our advertising columns, the second annual exhibition under the auspices of the Newton-le-Willows Horticultural Society will be held this (Saturday) afternoon. A splendid list of entries has been received, and with fine weather a success is assured. TILE EARLESTOWN FOOTBALL CL1513 AND THE BOLTON ENGINEERS DISPITTEL—The committee of the Earlestown Football Club have made arrangements for a match, the pro- ceeds of which will be devoted to the strike fund of the engineers at present on strike at Bolton. The full team of the Bolton Wanderers has promised to appear and meet a team selected from the local clubs. WARGRAVE Salton TEACHER'S PICNIC.—The annual picnic for the teachers of Wargrave Sunday school was held on Saturday, when a very pleasant day was spent at Llandudno. The company, numbering about 16, including a few friends, left Earlestown at seven o'clock in the morn- ing, and arrived at their destination about 10.30. During the day the party visited the varions paints of interest in the charming neighbourhood, and some engaged themselves in boating, while others bathed. The return journey was commenced about half-past six, and the friends arrived borne about ten o'clock, highly pleased with their day's outiog.

FUNERAL OF TRH LATE ALDERMAN CRAVEN.— The funeral of the late Alderman Craven took place on Thurs- day, at the churchyard at Warburton. The Manchester City Council and other public bodies were represented, and at the funeral service every seat in the church was oc- cupied. THE LICENSING SESSIONS.—At the annual Brewster Sessions held this week at Altrincham, the report of Super- intendent Leighton was read to the magistrates. It stated, amongst other matters, that in Lymm there are twelve li- censed victuallera ; five beerhouses licensed to sell on, and seven licensed to sell ff the premises; giving a total of 24 licensed houses fir Lymm, or one house to 188 inhabi- tants. .

_ VESTRY MEETING.—On Thursday morning a meeting in vestry of the parishioners of Lvmm was held in the Parish Church vsstry. the object of it being to consider a sugges- tion received by the Overseers of Lytnm from the Guar- dians of the Altrincham Union as to increasing the guarantee of the assistant overseer, and to make such provisions as might be deemed expedient. The Rector, the Rev. G. W. Guest, presided. The Altrincham Guardians recommended the vestry to increase the guarantee from £3OO to £5OO, which would entail an additional outlay of .£0 5s a year on the part of the assistant overseer.—The Assistant Overseer (Mr. Brazendale) stated that although his duties had in- creased to three times what they were in 1870, his salary had remained unaltered, and he thought that it would only be right that it should now be increased. He had, he re- marked, given every satisfaction in his position. and was also highly respected by the people of Lymtn—a good deal more so than many of those present. (Laughter.) It was only right and fair that his salary should be in- creased to the extent of the increased premium and the legal expenses connected with it —After a discussion it was resolved to make the following entry in the minute book : A communication from the Board if Guardians of the Al- trinchsm Union, with reference to increasing 010 guarantee of the assistant-overseer, suggesting a sum of £5OO, aid ad- vising that an additism of £6 5s be made to his annual salary, having bees read by the chairman, it was resolved— " That this recommendation be acted upon, and that Mr. Brazendall be required to find security to the above-named amount."

THE LYMM DROWNING CASE. A REMARKABLE COINCIDENCE.

Mr. Wori;le-y",;;;;;;,-Otr, Wednesday held an adjourned in- quiry on view of the body of Ann Rigby (52) a widow., whose dead body was recovered from the Bridgewater Canal I at Lymm early on the morning of the 16th instant. The inquiry was held at the Boll's Head Inn. It was opened on Wednesday week, when evidence was called that con- clusively proved that on the night of the 15th instant, when the annual Lymm Rushbearing festival was beieg observed, the deceased woman was seen in the village and on the Fair Ground by several persons, who unhesitatingly deposed that he was very much the worse for drink. On this point the evidence was complete. It was also deposed that while in conversation Os the night in question, with persons who were called as witnesses, the deceased con• ducted herself In a manner that led to the supposition that she was in a very despondent state of mind, as she was heard to remark that she was " put about," and would " bottom the water," and that " she would be found in the ranks of glory before to- marrow morning." As a matter of fact, her lifeless body was on the following morning discovered in the canal by a passing boatman, who awoke someone living near, and it was taken from the water. At the first in- quiry into the circumstances attending the death of the de- ceased, who was by trade a fustian cutter, it transpired that information had come to the knowledge of the police that made an adjournment advisable. On the resumption of the inquiry on Wednesday morning the Coroner said that at the previous inquiry evidence was taken at consider- able length. At the last moment he was informed by the polic,. that a man had on the same night that the woman was drowned in the canal got into the same canal, and that he was afterwards seen in a dripping wet condition in the same neighbourhood in which the deceased was drowned. That being the case, and that information not coming to the knowledge of the police in sufficient time for evidence regarding it to be called before the jury when the first in- quiry was held, he Rave an order for the burial of the body, proceeding to take all the material evidence that was then at the command of the police, and he then adjourned the Inquiry until that day its order that further inquiries might be made and fresh evidence produced to explain away the fact—if it could be explained away—or to elucidate the fact relating to this man, who no doubt was in the canal, as far as the information of the police went, at about the same time as was the deceased. The man was now to be called. He should call him before the jury, and caution him, and the evidence he would afterwards give would be before the jury. The witness, James Lewis by name, was then called. He said that he was a fustian cutter,and lived in Pepper-street, Lymm. Ile saw the deceased at about 11-20 p.m. on the night of tho 15th instant—Lymm Rushbearing. He was rather fresh, but not drunk.—The Coroner then cautioned the witness, and asked him had be any objection to relate what occurred on the night in question —Witness : I have nothing only myself. I only saw her when I gave her a copper te ride on the " bobby horses." The Coroner : Have you any objection to state what took place that nie ht?—Witness : No.—When did you last see leer? About 11-20; she was on the field. She was very fresh. and asked me if I would treat her on the " hobby horses," and I said Yes." I gave her 2d, $-ut did not go with her, as / went to the shooting gallery. I did not see her again that night. They put all the lights out, and I missed my way. That was about 12-30. I got against the gasworks wall,and I thought I was at Mr Holt's wall, I put my hand to the side and thought I could get into the lane, but I walked into the canal. I was in about twenty minutes struggling by myself. I called out many times. I got out of the canal without assistance, and knocked at the gas works wall. The niztat watchman came, and I asked him for a light, as it was very dark. He took me about half the way home, and then I said I could manage. I was not drunk.—Further examined, witness admitted that he was drunk et the time in question ; be was in Fair. dough's field when he got the aid of the watchman.—The Coroner : Had you any appointment to meet the deceased on this day? No.—When you say you did not again see her that night, you mean the whole night? I never saw her after 11-20 that night.—Peter Shaw, Sandy-lane, Lynam, a stoker at the gas works, was then called. He said that on the morning of the 18th instant he was at work when he hoard some one call out He got a lamp, and then saw John Lewis in John Lee's field. Lewis said, "Hello, Peter, is that you ? " and on witness replying that it was, Lewis said "I have been overhead in the cut," and asked witness to take him out of the 'field into the road. It was very dark, and Lewis could not find his way. He bad had drink, but was not "so bad."—Tne Coroner : He would have got sober through tnmbling in the water,l expect.— Witness, proceeding, said that Lewis did not explain how he had gat into the water, and did not say that he had been with anyone. It was not Fairclough's field that Lewis was in. It was in Lee's field, and if Lewis said otherwtse he was mistaken. Witness did not think Lewis was sober enough to know what he was doing, and he could not have fohnd his way out of the field. If witness had not supported him, he would have lain down. Lewis told him that he did not knew where he was, and when witness left him he (Lewis) stag- gered across the road.—The Coroner then briefly reviewed the evidence given at the first inquest, and said that the in- quiries made by the police had resulted in the discovery of the evidence that had just been called before the jury. He believed that both of the witnesses had given their evidence ' a satisfactory manner, and he believed that Lewis was really so. intoxicated that be did not know where he was, or what he was doing. If the jury thought that the woman, while drunk, got into the canal, and that by a coincidence the man also got into the canal, they would probably re- turn a verdict of found drowned, but if they thought any- upicion attached to Lewis they must again adjourn the injuiry.—A,ter a brief consultation, the jury returned ver- dict of" Found drowned," and stated their belief that
Lewis never saw the deceased after he paid for her to go on the " hobl y horses" en the Fair Ground.

lhe funeral service was impressively conducted by the Rev. H. A. Wolstenholme, who was assisted by the Rev. J. C. Pigot and the Rev. W. Smith. The remains were in- terred in the family vault in the Church of England por- tion; and during the service the site was surrounded by a very large number of sympathetic persons.

PULPIT The Rev. J. C. Pigot, vicar of St. Thomas' Church, preaching in that place • I worship on Sunday morning, referred to the death of Mr. Hall. He remarked that they were very sorry to think of his death, as be was one who always bore a kindly leeling towards all denominations, and afforded help whenever it was needed. He bad been a member of their church, and though he bad left them some years ago' he continued to show that kindly feeling to their church that he always did when with them. He was sure that they all sympathised with the deceased's family, and would have occasion to remember him as one who bad played well bis,part in life. The organist (Mr. J. S. Bate) at the conclusion of the service played Una "Dead March" in Saul, and special hymns were sung during the service.

RUNCORN WATERWORKS COMPANY. The annual meeting of the shareholders of the Runcorn, Weston. and Halton Waterworks Company was held in the Public Hall on Monday. Mr. J. Brundrit,J.P.,occupied the hair, and there were present Messrs. W. Hayes, W. Whit- taker, W. Bankes, E. Timmine, James Collier, P. Smith, F. Salkeld (secretary), and W. Jones (asaistant secretary). On the proposition of Mr. Collier, the statement of ac- counts was taken as read. The following is the report " The revenue account shows a balance of £729 Is 104 in- cluding £244 7s Id, brought from the previous half year, out of which the directors recommend a dividend to be de- Glared of four pounds per centum per annum, free from la- come tax, payable on and after the first day of Septem- ber. This will absorb £6OO, leaving a balance of £129 Is , 10d to be carried forward. The sand and debris which had Accumulated in the well, and the stones and materials left in it by the workmen at the time the borehole was made, have been effectually removed ;great advantage has thereby derived to the pumps and machinery. The directors found that it was absolutely necessary to present a petition to the committee of the House of Lords against the Liverpool Waterworks and Improvement Bill, 1887, so that the Run- corn, Weston, and Halton Waterworks Company might be protected from the Corporation supplying persons with water in the district of their Act of 1865. and support the same with evidence. The directors are able to inform the shareholders that they succeeded in obtaining a clause to he inserted in the Liverpool Waterworks and Improvement Bill, 1887. Prohibiting the Corporation from supplying water from their conduit pipe to any person or public body in the three townships of our Act. The water in the well continues abundant, the machinery and plant are in good working order, and the buildings in substantial repair." The Chairman movenhe adoption of the report. and that a dividend at the rate of 4 per cent, per annum be paid. Al- luding to the clearing of the well, the chairman said divers were employed, and 16 to 20 tons of sand and debris of one sort of another had been removed by mesas of buckets. As they might imagine the process was a very slow one, an& the total cost of the work was about £lOO. After careful consideration the directors decided that half of that amouct should be charged to capital account, and half to revenue account. He then proceeded to explain what had been done as to the Liverpool Waterworks Bill. The directors made inquiry, and found that it was not so much this Bill, but other bills in connection with it, in which there were clauses which would enable the Corporation to provide water to any works in Runcorn by making an agreement with them, and so cut the ground from under the feet of the company. It was quite to the company's interest, and necessary that they should oppose this clause. They did so In the House of Lords, and succeeded in obtaining a clause which prevented the Corporation supplying water within the Company's district without their consent in writing. The directors considered that a sufficient safeguard for the future, and that the company was put on a more sound basis. The Commissioners could do nothing unless they first acquired the Company's rights or got the Company's permission. The directors had no wish to oppose the Com- missioners in any way, and they were of one mind that it was not necessary for the Commissioners to help the Corpo- ration in opposing the Company. No doubt the expenses would be heavy. Anybody that bad any acquaintance with Parliamentary work must know that it was not done for nothing, but they had not got the account from London, and therefore were unable to give an approximate of the amount. The company would have had their interests very much prejudiced, if not entirely destroyed, if they bad not taken this action. Mr. W. Heyes seconded the motion. Mr. Timmins remarked that it would be gratifying to the shareholders to know that during this season of almost unprecedented drought, when corporations and water companies had been shutting off water 12 hours out of the 24, there had been an abundant supply of water. This fact would add to the value of the company, and be thought they had reason to be proud of the waterworks. (Hear, hear.) The motion was carried unanimously. Mr. Brundrit and Mr. Whittaker, the retiring directors were unanimously re-elected. In responding to a vote of thanks the chairman observe& that they would not want any water from the Liverpool Corporation for many years to come.
