The water famine is being severely felt in Ulster. Several mills have recently been stopped. The bankruptcy was on Friday announced In the Kirk- cudbright's Sherffs Court of Captain Maxwell Heron, late M.P. for Kirkcudbright. The "Freeman's Journal" of Friday says the Lord- Lieutenant and party were hissed mast vigorously at the horse show on Thursday. A strong southerly gale, accompanied with heavy rain, has been blowing off Queenstown since Thursday night. Steamers coming in report severe weather outside. . .
_ At a meeting at North Hunts' on Thursday, it was an- nounced that Mr. T. W. Russell, M.P.' had offered to speak in support of Mr. Sanders, the Ciladetcnian can- didate.

Ate ENORMOrS SALMOIC—The largest salmon takep in the Dee for several years was secured early on Friday morn- ing by a Chester fisherman. When scaled it weighed 481 b. It is a male fish, and in splendid condition. By a fire at midnight, on Thursday, on the premises of Mr. J D. Rohirmn, carting agent to the Great Western Railway at Sbeffi.ld, 13 horses, valued at £7OO, were burnt to death,the stables and stores of provender being totally consumed. MEETING OF IRISH Leurtmoups.—The Duke of Aber- cern presided at a meeting of landlords, on Friday, in Dub- lin, held for the purpose of organising a deputation to wait upon the Government to urge the claims of the landlords to their consideration.

TRE QUEEN AND NORTE WALES.—At Friday's sitting of the National Provincial Eisteddfod, at Portmadec, Mr. Oakley, the president, announced, amidst loud cheering, that he had it on the best authority that the Queen would next year visit North Wales. THREE MEN SIIFF9CAFED.—WhiIat discharging a cargo of paper and rags from the Christian IX, belonging to London, at Copenhagen, on Thursday. three men were suf- focated on entering the hold, owing to the poisonous vapours which had accumulated therein. Death was instan- taneous.

DEATH OF LORD DONERAILE FROM HYDROPHOBIA -- A Mallow correspondent telegraphs that Lord Doneraile died on Friday morning, at Doneraile, county Cork, from the effects of hydrophobia, resulting from the bite of a pet fcr last January. Lord Doneraile was in his seventieth year, and was an Irish representative peer. DESTRUCTIVE RAILWAY COLLISION,—AbOIIt two O'clock on Friday morning a bank engine ran into a train of empty coaches at Bridgend, Glamorganshire, smashing the rearmost to pieces, and seriously damaging several other coaches. The engine was likewise badly damaged, and the driver of the colliding engine was seriously shakes.

THE BOLTON STRIKE.—The committee issued on Ftiday their fifteenth weekly balance sheet, which shows on the receipt side an income of £1,723 124. towards which Man- chester contributes .£4O, Oldham £2O, Bury £3l, Blackburn £25, London £3O, Woolwich £l3, and local contributions .£l2B The expenditure, which is heavy now, owing to the society men receiving 5s 64 extra, and the non-society men 2's 6d. is £451, leaving a favourable balance of £1,282. Gnnar FIRE IN GLASGOW.—A fire occurred on Friday morning in Glasgow in ths extensive wholesale upholstery works of Messrs Cumming and Smith, Wallace-street. The cabinet section was destroyed. When the wall facing Kyle- st,eet fell many firemen had narrow escapes. Steamers ' were playing upon the flames for a considerable time, as the materials burning were of a very inflammable nature. The damage is estimated at vpoo, Over /70 men will be thrown out of employment. Snoextrrn TRAGEDY IN DERBYSHIRE —An extraordinary. scene was witnessed on the highway near Bakewell, Derby- shire, on Thursday night. Patrick Mulvey, a hawker, and his son were thrown from their cart, and the father fell into the river Wye. Both men were under the influence of drink. A gentleman driving past tried to rescue Mulvey, but the latter was dead when got out. The son then tried to drown himself, bet was prevented. He afterwards took a dose of laudanum, but his life was saved by the adminis- tration of an emetic. The wife of the deceased, on arriving at the scene, wanted to rush into the river with her child, and was with difficulty restrained by the police. GREAT FIRE AT STOCKPORT.—EarIy on Friday morning a great fire occurred at the People's Opera House, Stock- port. The building was left apparently all safe at 11 o'clock, but about mid-night the policeman on duty in the rear heard crackling, and discovered the building to be on fire. He at once gave alarm, and the Corporation and West of England Brigade were soon on the spot. The fire at- tracted a great crowd. A later telegram says :—The interior of the theatre is a mass of ruins, charred timber lying in every direction, the vicinity of the stage being a mass of destroyed properties. The damage is estimated at from £1,500,t0 £2,000. and is covered by insurance in the Phenix Office. Fortunately all the musical instruments were saved. Mr. Revill is the proprietor of theatres at Ashton-under-Lyne, St. Helens, and Macclesfield, and his son-in-law conducts those at Rochdale and Bury.

A terrible accident which, it is feared, resulted in the loss of 14 or 15 lives occurred off Ilfracombe, on Friday afternoon, the yacht Monarch, which runs excursions daily in the Channel, left in the afternoon with about n persons and two boatman on board. A squall struck the vessel as
TRAGIC SUICIDE AT ST. HELENS.-
SWALLOWING CARBOLIC ACID.

On Tuesday night and Wednesday morning a great deal of excitement was manifested in St. Helens by a report that a man had committed suicide by swallowing a dose of carbolic acid undet circumstances of a tragical nature. The report proved to be well founded, and the facts show that the deed was premeditated. The deceased man was named Alexander Lockhart, and at the time of his death he was living at his mother's- house, y, Barton-street. He was 26 years of age, and was employed as a joiner at the bottle- works of Messrs. Cannington, Shaw. and Company. Up to about three weeks ago, and /or a few years past, the de- ceased, who was unmarried, bad cohabited with a married woman who resided near Messrs. Pilkington's glassworks. It is stated that about three weeks ago the parties quarrelled and the deceased left his paramour. Oa Saturday night last the parties met in a public-house, and after some words had passed the deceased struck the woman. On the Monday morning she took out a summons against the deceased on a charge of assault, and this summons directing him to appear at the Town Hall on Friday (yesterday) was served upon him by the police on Tuesday morning. It is alleged that upon its receipt the deceased said he would not live throughout the day, and this ex- pression was carried into effect. About half-past six o'clock the deceased entered the shop of Mr. Samuel Wilson, chemist and druggist, Duke-street, and asked for three-pennyworth of carbolic; acid. This was supplied by an assistant, and the deceased left the shop. Immediately on getting to the door the deceased raised the bottle to tae lips and drank nearly half the liquid in the bottle. It is said he immediately exclaimed "I've poisoned myself," and several persons, including his mother, ran to his assis- tance. In wresting the bottle from her son's hands Lock hart had her hands and arms severely burned. The de- ceased,.who was badly burned and scalded about the mouth and throat, was taken to his mother's home and Dr. Marsh was at once sent for. The doctor appeared quickly upon the spot, but the deceased was past all help, and he eme. pired about half an hour after committing the rash act. It is stated that the deceased has been drinking heavily during the past three weeks. THE INQUEST. _ . _

An inquest on the body of the deceased was held at the Town Ball, on Friday morning, before Mr S Brighouse,. coroner.—Henry Eatock, assistant to Mr Wilson, said when deceased purchased the poison, he asked him if be knew how to Use it. Deceased replied that he did,as he had had it many a time.—Mr Wilson said the Poisons Act did no affect carbolic acid, so long as the bottle was labelled " Poison," as the bottle in question was. They had done all the Act required in regard to the matter —The jury returned a verdict of "Suicide whilst temporarily insane." It is. stated that deceased's father committed suicide.

div.head: LETTER FROM IRELAND.
div.p: A LETTER FROM IRELAND.
To the Editor of "The Examiner." Sir,—The following is a copy of a letter sent to me by a Nationalist town councillor for an impor- tant town in Tipperary county.—Yours, T. W.

Runcorn, 2fith August, 1887. [coPv.] My Dear Nephew,—l received your post card and telegram also, announcing the result of your late victory at Northwich, and, owing to my uncertain business hours, I was not able to answer it sooner. I , must say that the decision of Northwich Division has been the crowning success of Home Rule, but I need not tell you that it is nothing but what we expected from the gallant Tipperary boys, who are never backward in the fight for freedom to every man, no matter who or what he may be. We have had a proclamation posted on the Market House here to-day prohibiting any more meetings of the Irish National League, but we will snap our fingers at them. I think the death knell of the Coercion Tory Jubilee Government has been sounded when "Londonderry" sent his liame to. decorate the en- trance to the R.I.C. walls and Petty Sessions Court House doors here. I hope you have seen the report of the meeting at the Rotunda, in Dublin. It was a complete success. Your representatives were the crowning stars, especially Mr. Cobb, whom I think , is more Irish than the Irish themselves.

I wish to remark to you that there was no occa- sion for coercion this year, as the season coerced the farmers well enough when they had to bring their cattle four Sr five miles to get a drink of water. I hope you -will make up your mind to make us a flying visit soon, and help to stir up a true spirit of conciliation between the English and Irish nations. We only want conciliation. We want to be friendly, but we must get our rights. This, I assure you, is the earnest wish of every true Irish- man the world over. Hoping yourself and family, and all my friends, are well, in haste I remain, I yours truly and sincere uncle, THOS. AIIERN.

div.head: WOOLTON VILLAGE CLUB SPORTS.
div.p: WOOLTON VILLAGE CLUB SPORTS.

The third annual amateur athletic sports, under the aus- pices of the Woolton Village Club, were held on Thursday at Wootton, in a field lent for the occasion by Mr. Alfred Fletcher, J.P. The popularity of the sports is testified by the fact that the entries were in excess of last year,and much larger than those of Ike first year. Mr W Sandbrook offi- ciated as starter, Dr Scott, Meters J Salon, and A Wood as Judges, while Mr H P Ellis discharged the duties of handi- capper and referee with efficiency. Messrs J Mearsh, R Kershaw, 1) Wainwright, jun., and C Ryland s were the clerks of the course. There was a large concourse of spectators, and the proceedings were enlivened by the spirited performances of the Widnes Soap Works brass band, under the able leadership of Mr William Jennett. The various events were well contested, and the presence of a number of boys who took part in the running was a feature of the proceedings. THE LATE MR. H. S. HALL, J.P.-FUNERAL AT

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.

The interment of the remains of Mr. H. S. Hall, JP, of Windle Grange, St. Helens, and a partner in the firm of Maser,. Hall Brothers, and Shaw, chemical manufacturers, Widnes, took place :at St. Helens cemetery at noon on Tuesday. The general respect in which the deceased gen- tleman was held by all classes of the community was evi- denced by the attendance of magistrates, clergymen, and gentlensen of all shades of political opinions and religious beliefs, while many poor and aged men and women tramped to the place of interment, and manifested their sorrow at the loss of a sympathetic and generous fried in an affect. ing manner. Long before the hour announced for the sad ceremony people began to gather at the cemetery and its vicinity. Shortly before twelve the funeral cortege left the late residence of the deceased gentleman. First came a I number of the employee of Messrs. Hall Brothers, and Shaw (Widnes), the clerks, , from the office of Messrs. Ansdell and Eccles (solicitors, St. Helens), and they were followed by the tenamts and farmers on the Windle Grange estate. Next were Messrs. Middlehurst, Ranson, Unsworth, Robinson, W. Swift. Grant, Ark- wright, Robinson, Hurst, and other gentlemen re- presenting the Windle Highway Board (of which deceased had been chairman for some years), the School At- tendance Committee, Windle Dole Charity, cte. Next came a considerable number of local gentlemen, amongst whom were Mr. A. Walmsley, J.P., Mr. Councillor J. Forster, Messrs. H, Martin. H. R. Lacey, J. Lewis, J. B. Leach, B. A. Dromgoole, James Burchall. George Webster, Mr. Marsh dfc. A carriage containing the officiating clergy- men, followed. Their names were—Rev. H. A. Wolsten- holme (senior curate St. Helens Parish Cherch), Rev. J. C. Pigot (vicar of St. Thomas's Church, Bt. Helens), Rev. W, Smith (vicar of Christ Church, Pennington, near Leigh), and Rev. W. Flaherty (vicar of Holy Trinity Church, Parr.) The hearse, an elegant one, with glass sides, through which the coffin, covered with wreaths, could be seen, followed. The hearse was succeeded by five mourn- ing coaches containing the mourners and immediate rela- tives as under :—let, Mr. and Mrs Radcliffe Hall, Miss Laura Hall (of Bedford), and Mr. Arthur Hall (Weybridge); 2nd, Mr. Ralph Hall (Bedford), Mr. W. Hall, Mr.W. C. Eccles, and Mr. J. S. Eccles ; 3rd, Mr. George Hall, Mr. George, Turner (Southport), Mr. Robert Shaw (Widnes), and Mr. J. Cross Eccles; 4th, Mr. John Marsh, Mr. Chas. Snaps, Mr. William Marsh, and Mr. E. Pierpoint ; sth, Dr. E. P. Twyferd, J.P., Dr. Dalton, Mr. Fogg, and Mr. James Marsh. The rear of the mournful procession was 4 brought up by 28 private carriages, amongst the ladies and gentlemen marking their respect in this manner being the Mayor (Colonel Gamble), Lieutenant-Colonel Richard Pil- kington (Rainford Hall), Mr. A. Walmesley, J.P., Mr. Jos. Robinson, Miss Bishop. Mr. C. J. Bishop, J.P., Dr. E. P. Twvford, J.P., Dr. Jamison, Mr. W. Blinkborn, J.P., Dr. McNic3ll, Rev. Howard St. George Offillinge), Mr. Henry Baxter (Rainhill), Mr William Gamble (Haresfinch), Alder- man J C Gamble (Cowley Hill), Dr Gasket', J.P., Mr W Richardson (Rainford), dm. The blinds along the route to the cemetery were all drawn, and large numbers of people congregated at various points. At the cemetery a large mimber of gentlemen bad congregated, amongst wham were Alderman J Harrison, J.P., Alderman D McKechnie, Coun- cillors A Hanson, C J Bishop ; Mr J H Craik (deputy town clerle„ Mr G Davison (magistrates' clerk) ; Rev A A Nunn, Rev H A Arnold, Rev G Lakeman, Rev J Pick- well, ; Dr IVlcNicoll-; Messrs R Belsher, A J Speeden, W Gamble, J Hammill, J Robinson, J Boyden, W Marsh, A Carr, H S Oppeelfeim, J Goldsworth, J Loader, A Smith (Widnes), S Robinson (Widnes), C E Finney (Liverpool), James Galloway (Liverpool), and others. The body of the deceased gentleman was enclosed in a metallic shell with an outer covering of oak, with brass mountings and fittings. On a brass shield plate was the inscription "Henry Samuel Hall, died August 18th, 1887,1 aged 65 years." The coffin was literally covered with splendid wreaths, amongst the contributors being Mr and Mrs Radclvffe Hall, Mr Ralph and the Misses Hall, Miss Hall, Miss Cross, Mrs Arthur Hall, Miss Grace Hall, Mr and Mrs William Cross Eccles, Mr J S Eccles, Mm George Turner, Mr and Mrs R Shaw, Mr and Mrs Pierpoint, Miss Pierpoint, Mr and Mrs Page (Sussex), Mr A Walmsley Miss Bishop, Rev J C Pigot, Mr J Davies, Mr J Golds- worth, Mrs Hammill, Mr George Webster. Mr T T Hayes, J.P., and Mr and Mrs Cripps. A. magnificent wreath, prin- cipally of white lilies, had attached to it a card bearing the following inscription :—" From St. Helens Liberals, in kindly and grateful remembrance of the long, active, and generous labour in the people's cause, of Henry Samuel Hall, Escle J.P., and sincere sympathy with Mrs Hall and the family." This was presented by a deputation of Liberals, comprising Messrs .1 Forster, H Martin, J Boy- dell, and B A Dromgoole. There were also wreaths horn the choir and friends of the Primitive Methodist Chapel, , Westfield-atreet, the tenantry, and the servants at Vdi,ndle 1 Grange.

LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS. The Hose met at half-past four o clock. MISCELEANEOUS.—Numerous I:editions against vivisection were presented. The Savings Rank. and Government annul. , ties, and Sheriff of Lanarkshire Bills were read a second time. The Scotch Public Libraries Acts Amendments Bill passed through committee. The House adjourned at 20 minutes to five until Tuesday. HOUSE OF COMMONS. The House met at four o'clock. QuEsrlous.—Baron de WORMS, replying to Mr. Hoare, said the Board of Trade were not inclined to make experi- ments with the use of oil in stormy weather at sea.—Sir J. FERGUSON, replying to Mr. Baden Powell, said be could , give no information as to the course of action relative to the proposed International Conference en the sugar bounty question until the answers of Foreign Powers were received. —Sir T. FERGUSON, replying to Mr. Legh, said it was quite true Ayoub Khan had left Teheran ; his destination was unknown. He could give no information on the subject.— Mr.W. SMITH, replying to Mr. Burt, said the Mines Bill would be taken when the Civil Service Estimates were completed and the Allotment Bill passed through committee. The Indian Budget would not be brought forward next week.—The H'ostis SECRETARY, replying to a question as to the continued imprisonment of five persons at Leicester, said the imprisonment was not fir preaching, but for ob- structing the highway, and the question to be determined WAS whether the market place was a public highway.—Ad- journed debate on Mr. Gladstone's motion for address against the pioclamation of tbe National League was resumed. THE ADJOURNED DEBATE. Sir GEORGE TREVELYAN supported the address. He said he was glad be had returned to the House when he could utilize the information he gained when he was secretary for Ireland. He pointed out that when coercive measares were asked by Lord Spencer, the fullest information as to crime and outrages was given to Parliament, and everything he (Sir George) stated was grounded on published statements, but that could not be said to have been done in the present caee. He insisted that when that House was asked to sanc- tion the proclamation of the National League, the fullest information ought to be given; because if the proclamation , was sanctioned every Irishman who belonged to the League and refused to leave it would be liable to be published as a criminal, and that would not depend upon any judicial pro- ceeding, because every person who WAS taken before the resident magistrates would be sent to prison and that with- out trial. Before the League was proclaimed it might to have been stated the number and condition of its branches, the number of outrages, and ether information, but nothing of the kind had, been made known, and Parliament was asked to take the step in the absence of such information. That was a proceeding to which he entertained the strongest objection, and he protested in the strongest manner against the course pursued by the Government. He demanded from the ministers a clear declaration of the purposes to which they proposed to put the proclamation, the process by which they proposed to carry out the powers they were taking, and the limit to which they would restrict them, though be was afraid before they had been long possessed of the powers they would find themselves unable to put any limit on them. A Government which took power to treat it& political opponents as criminals would as history taught, be obliged sooner or later to use that Power, and the result would be trouble which could net be foreseen. The Arrourenv-GiorznAL defended the policy of the Government, and replying to the charge made by Mr. Gladstone of political imposition, he insisted that that Ins- posture existed on the Opposition side of the House, because they declined to walk six yards to find out the state of things that prevailed in Ireland. Therefore they assumed that crime and outrage did not exist, and that the Govern- ment were guilty of oppression in taking the course they felt called upon to adopt. Mr. T. LIABRINGTON as officially responsible for the action of the National League, defended that organisation from the charges that had been brought against it. He strongly denied that it sympathised with crime or aided OS abetted it, and he gave an emphatic contradiction to the allegation that it interfered with the administration of that law, or that it incited to intimidation. He insisted that an organisation more extensive than had ever before ex- isted in Ireland, and expressive of the opinions of the peo- ple it represented more than any like association in Europe, was not to be condemned upon anonymous stories, the truth of which there had been no opportunity of testing. The discussion haying been continued by Mr. Iliacartney and M. Redmond, Lord HARTINOMON. said he thought the House would have heard with some surprise Slr O. Trevelyan's approval of some portions of the Crimes Act, and he questioned whether he would have received the support of the elec- tor& of the Bridgeton division of Glasgow if it had been known that he approved of the Crimes Act lust passed. The point before the House was not the connection of the National League with crime and outrage in Ireland, but whether intimidation was practised and prevailed to such an extent as to have produced absolute submission. The right hon. Bart. had not denied that intimidation had ex- lewd, but has argued that the Government ought to have followed the course adopted by Lord Spencer; but the Go- vernment of Lord Spencer old not put an end to intimida- tion, and it was equally true that after the lapse of the pro- visions of the Crimes Act intimidation greatly increased, and that tyranny was more urgent, more frequent, and more organised than at any former period . The House divided with the following result : For Mr. Gladstone's resolution Against
